claims.text: You cannot get rich by renting out your time; wealth requires owning equity in a business, product or asset
claims.note: Wealth surveys show most large fortunes come from business ownership and assets, but high-earning salaried professionals do accumulate wealth by saving and investing.

claims.text: There are no get-rich-quick schemes; whoever sells one is getting rich off the buyer
claims.note: FTC business-opportunity cases and MLM income disclosures consistently show the seller profits while most buyers lose money, though rare individual windfalls exist.

claims.text: Advice from people who got rich quickly is survivorship bias, like reading out winning lottery numbers
claims.note: Survivorship bias is well documented; the specific path of a rapid success rarely replicates because luck and timing dominated it.

claims.text: Get-rich advice from someone whose income comes mainly from selling that advice is suspect
claims.note: Nudge's $400 million came from selling real-estate training, and over 95% of its seminar attendees lost money net; consistent with the heuristic for this scheme.

claims.text: Self-made wealth accumulates slowly through compounding over a decade or more, not in one big payout
claims.note: Most self-made millionaires reach it in their 40s and 50s after decades of accumulation, though tech exits give a minority lumpy, lottery-like outcomes.

claims.text: Code and media scale without labor or capital, so they are where new fortunes are made
claims.note: Zero-marginal-cost products underlie many recent fortunes, but building them takes labor and often capital, and outcomes are power-law with most participants earning little.

claims.text: Making money is a learnable skill, not luck; a skilled person could rebuild wealth from nothing within a decade
claims.note: Skill raises the odds, but research on entrepreneurial and wealth outcomes finds a large luck component, so neither 'not luck' nor a reliable decade-long rebuild holds.

claims.text: Only knowledge that cannot be taught in a classroom earns outsized pay; trainable skills get commoditized to the cost of training
claims.note: Scarce, hard-to-codify skills do earn a premium, but many trainable credentialed professions still pay very well because entry is restricted.

claims.text: Nobody sustains high-output work at 80-plus hours a week; output per hour collapses and the brain breaks down
claims.note: Pencavel's munitions-worker data and later studies show output per hour falls steeply beyond about 50 hours a week.

claims.text: Entrepreneurs accept frequent small losses for rare big wins and earn more than employees on average
claims.note: Incorporated entrepreneurs have much fatter-tailed earnings than salaried workers (the 90th-percentile incorporated earns 70% more than the 90th-percentile salaried worker) and average 48% higher residual hourly earnings, but the aggregate median self-employed earns about 15% less and the median unincorporated owner about 30% less than comparable employees, and the authors do not assess risk-adjusted returns or losses; 'earn more on average' holds for incorporated entrepreneurs, not business owners generally.

claims.text: Never bet everything on one gamble even with an edge, because ruin removes you from the game
claims.note: Kelly-criterion and ergodicity arguments show that full-stake bets with positive expectation still go bust with probability approaching one over repeated play.

claims.text: Wealth creation is positive-sum, so everyone can become wealthy
claims.note: Total wealth grows, but being wealthy is largely relative and scarce assets are constrained, so positive-sum growth does not mean everyone can become wealthy.

claims.text: Most side-hustle ideas can be launched for a few hundred dollars using free trials and free marketplaces
claims.note: Many service and digital side hustles can launch for a few hundred dollars, though unpaid time and customer acquisition are the real costs.

claims.text: Any side hustle can be scaled into a multi-million-dollar business
claims.note: Most small businesses never grow past a handful of employees, so scaling any side hustle to millions is a rare exception.

claims.text: Copying an already-working business model exactly beats trying to differentiate at launch
claims.note: Imitation lowers idea risk, but entering a proven niche means facing incumbents, and studies comparing imitators with innovators show mixed survival.

claims.text: Going full-time on a side hustle multiplies its income far beyond the extra hours because commitment forces it to work
claims.note: Survivor anecdotes aside, people who quit jobs for ventures often see income fall, and commitment does not create demand.

claims.text: Genuinely passive income is rare and only becomes possible after years of active, unglamorous income
claims.note: Passive income almost always requires accumulated capital or an operating business first; income disclosures from passive-income pitches show most buyers earn little.

claims.text: Paid social ads are a learnable skill in days and a money machine for any product
claims.note: Ad platforms are easy to use but hard to profit from, and many small advertisers never reach a positive return.

claims.text: Selling AI automation setups to local small businesses is a viable low-capital service business because owners want AI but lack time to implement it
claims.note: It is a low-capital service and owners do show interest in AI, but demand, pricing and retention for one-person agencies are unproven.

claims.text: Drop-servicing, a marketing front-end that subcontracts local service work, earns margin without doing or knowing the work
claims.note: Lead arbitrage exists, but ad costs, licensing, liability and contractor quality make margin without knowing the work unreliable for most.

claims.text: Scraped directory websites can earn passive ad or lead income for near-zero cost; it is a numbers game across many sites
claims.note: Search engines demote thin scraped and aggregator sites, so most such directories earn nothing and are not passive.

claims.text: A vending machine route can be started with a used machine for a few hundred dollars and returns depend mostly on location
claims.note: Used machines are cheap and location drives returns, but a typical machine nets modest sums and restocking is ongoing labor.

claims.text: Small RV or mobile-home parks bought with seller financing are many times more profitable than single-family rentals
claims.note: Park yields run somewhat higher than single-family rentals for more work and risk, not many times higher, and low-cash seller financing is rare.

claims.text: Entrepreneurship is often more of a prison than a 9-to-5 in its early years; the freedom narrative is oversold
claims.note: Self-employed people report longer hours, lower median income and higher financial stress than employees in most surveys.

claims.text: Thinly traded prediction markets are cheap to manipulate, so their odds can be bought as a PR tool
claims.note: Documented manipulation attempts moved odds temporarily, but studies find manipulated prices usually revert and markets still forecast about as well as polls.

claims.text: Retail bettors on prediction markets face quantitative market-making firms, a structural disadvantage research cannot close
claims.note: Professional market makers do capture spread from retail flow, but retail traders with genuine information edges can still win; no data isolates retail returns on these platforms.

claims.text: Venues that attract retail money follow a sharks-and-fish cycle: professionals extract from amateurs until amateurs quit and liquidity collapses
claims.note: Online poker's mid-2000s decline fits the pattern, though regulation drove much of it; whether prediction markets follow the same path is untested.

claims.text: Prediction-market exchanges are structurally fairer than sportsbooks because the platform is not the counterparty and does not limit winners
claims.note: Sportsbooks demonstrably limit or close winning accounts, while exchanges match peers for a fee, though exchanges can still delist markets or change resolution rules.

claims.text: Insider trading is common on prediction markets and is defended by proponents as improving price accuracy
claims.note: Several documented cases of bets placed on non-public military and political information exist and the defence is openly made; overall prevalence is unknown.

claims.text: Legalising online betting in a jurisdiction lowers household credit scores and raises bankruptcies and delinquencies
claims.note: The paper measures balance sheets, not credit scores or bankruptcies: after legalization low-savings households carry about $368 (8%) more credit card debt, lose available credit and more often max out cards, and the authors cite a concurrent credit-bureau study (Hollenbeck et al. 2024) finding worse credit health, bankruptcy and delinquency among lower-income households.

claims.text: Prediction markets raise no capital for productive use; they only transfer money from retail bettors to platforms, quants and insiders
claims.note: They do not fund businesses, but their forecasts are an information good used by media and hedgers, so pure transfer is not the whole picture.

claims.text: Young people turn to get-rich-quick bets because traditional wealth-building paths feel out of reach
claims.note: Nearly 40% of crypto-app users are men under 35 (26% of the general population) and they respond most to price run-ups, but the paper attributes this to risk-seeking and a speculative motive and never tests whether traditional wealth paths feel out of reach.

claims.text: Proof-of-work mining rewards whoever can buy the most hardware and electricity, so returns concentrate with existing capital
claims.note: Mining economics scale with capital and cheap power; hash rate is dominated by large industrial operations and pools.

claims.text: Profits taken out of crypto tokens can only come from later buyers paying in more, so token speculation is zero- or negative-sum in dollars
claims.note: True for pure token trading net of fees and mining costs, but overstated for assets with any real utility or cash flow.

claims.text: Most NFTs only point to an off-chain image that can be altered or lost, so the token confers no durable ownership of the artwork
claims.note: Most ERC-721 metadata referenced HTTP or IPFS URLs; link rot and swapped images were documented repeatedly.

claims.text: NFT resale royalties are enforced by marketplaces rather than the token, so they are easily bypassed
claims.note: Major marketplaces made creator royalties optional in 2022-2023 and royalty income collapsed, confirming they were never on-chain enforced.

claims.text: Most artists who minted NFTs lost money on fees while gains went to early crypto holders and whales
claims.note: Market analyses found most NFTs sold for trivial sums or not at all and trading was concentrated among a small set of wallets, though a minority of artists did earn meaningful sums.

claims.text: Wash trading, where sellers buy from their own wallets to fake demand, is rampant in NFT markets
claims.note: Blockchain analytics firms found wash trades made up a large share of NFT volume on several marketplaces in 2021-2022.

claims.text: NFT project communities police doubt as FUD, so scrutiny of a project's viability is suppressed
claims.note: A description of community norms and framing rather than a measurable outcome.

claims.text: Blockchain transfers are irreversible and no authority can return stolen tokens, so scam victims have no recourse
claims.note: Transactions are final by design; recovery depends on marketplace delisting, ransom or rare exchange cooperation.

claims.text: A failed NFT mint still pays its creators, so projects have little incentive to deliver what they promise
claims.note: Mint proceeds are collected up front and rug pulls were common, though reputational effects do push some teams to deliver.

claims.text: Play-to-earn game economies need an endless inflow of new players to hold token prices up, so earnings collapse once growth stalls
claims.note: The leading play-to-earn game's reward token lost most of its value in 2022 once new-player growth stopped.

claims.text: Play-to-earn scholarship schemes let account owners take a large cut of players' earnings, leaving players at or below local minimum wage
claims.note: Reporting and economy analyses documented sub-minimum-wage earnings after the 2021 downturn, though earlier earnings had briefly exceeded local wages.

claims.text: Transaction fees on popular blockchains make them impractical for everyday purchases
claims.note: Accurate for Ethereum mainnet and Bitcoin at the time; later layer-2 networks and other chains cut fees to cents.

claims.text: Crypto pump-and-dump groups recruit retail participants who end up being the ones dumped on
claims.note: Studies of Telegram and Discord pump groups found organizers and early insiders profit while later participants lose.

claims.text: Years to financial independence depend only on savings rate, not on income level
claims.note: Mathematically true under constant real returns and equal spending before and after, but low incomes hit a fixed-cost floor that limits achievable savings rates.

claims.text: Cutting spending shortens time to retirement more than raising income because it both raises savings and lowers the amount needed
claims.note: A permanent spending cut reduces the required nest egg and raises the savings rate at once, which the retirement arithmetic confirms.

claims.text: An ordinary earner who saves a large majority of take-home pay can reach financial independence in about a decade
claims.note: The savings-rate math holds under reasonable return assumptions; the claim is conditional on actually saving a large majority, which is the hard part but not a false promise.

claims.text: A 4% inflation-adjusted withdrawal rate lets a portfolio sustain spending indefinitely
claims.note: 4% survived most historical US periods, but it was tested for 30 years; over open-ended horizons and in non-US data failure rates rise unless spending flexes.

claims.text: Stocks reliably return about five percent a year above inflation over the long run
claims.note: Global equities have averaged about this real return over a century, but 'reliably' overstates it given multi-decade stretches of near-zero real returns.

claims.text: Paying down a mortgage early is a risk-free return equal to the mortgage rate
claims.note: Avoided interest is a guaranteed pre-tax return at the loan rate, less any lost interest deduction.

claims.text: Retirement accounts can be tapped before the standard age without penalty through substantially equal periodic payments
claims.note: US tax code section 72(t) allows penalty-free SEPP withdrawals; Roth conversion ladders are another route.

claims.text: Expected real returns from high starting valuations are below historical averages, so early-retirement timelines built on historical returns are optimistic
claims.note: Valuation measures like CAPE have modest predictive power for 10-year returns, though realized 2012-2022 US returns beat those forecasts.

claims.text: Rental property bought well can yield more after inflation than a stock portfolio
claims.note: Unlevered total returns to US single-family rentals, 1986-2014, were about 8.5% a year across cities, similar to average equity returns rather than above them, with lower-price-tier zip codes earning higher total returns, so well-chosen cheaper rentals can edge out but the asset class as a whole matches stocks.

claims.text: Early retirees must budget for rising health costs and variable expenses that a fixed-spending model ignores
claims.note: Health spending rises with age and children's costs vary, though work-related expenses fall after retirement, so the net effect is uncertain.

claims.text: Investors' realized returns lag the funds they hold because they sell in downturns
claims.note: Investor-return studies consistently find a behavior gap of roughly one to two percentage points a year from poorly timed flows.

claims.text: Most retail day traders lose money
claims.note: Individual investors who day traded in Taiwan from 1992 to 2006: aggregate day-trader performance is negative and the vast majority of day traders are unprofitable, many persisting despite long experience of losses.

claims.text: Practicing in a simulator before trading real money improves a trader's odds
claims.note: Simulators teach mechanics and can screen out losing strategies, but they omit slippage and emotion and the large majority of day traders still lose money.

claims.text: Once a trader has a consistently profitable setup, profits scale by simply increasing position size
claims.note: Liquidity, slippage and market impact erode edges as size grows, especially in thin small caps, so profits do not scale by simply sizing up.

claims.text: Targeting trades that pay twice what is risked lets a trader be wrong most of the time and still profit
claims.note: The arithmetic is correct, but win rate falls as reward targets widen, so a 2:1 target does not by itself make a trader profitable.

claims.text: Low-float stocks gapping up on news with unusually high volume produce the largest intraday moves
claims.note: Low-float momentum stocks do show the largest percentage moves, but they are also the stocks most associated with retail losses and promotional manipulation.

claims.text: After a breaking-news surge, the first pullback is usually bought and offers a low-risk entry
claims.note: Short-horizon momentum continuation exists in the literature, but there is no independent evidence that this specific pattern is profitable for retail traders after costs.

claims.text: Losses trigger revenge trading that compounds losses in an emotional feedback loop
claims.note: Behavioral-finance studies document loss-chasing and increased risk-taking after losses among retail traders.

claims.text: A guru's documented profits do not predict the results of students who copy the strategy
claims.note: Survivorship bias and the base rate of trader losses mean an instructor's record says little about student outcomes.

claims.text: Reviewing one's own trade history reveals price ranges and times of day where the trader is profitable, which can be used to refine a strategy
claims.note: Journaling helps spot costly habits, but slicing a small sample of trades for winning subsets mostly finds noise.

claims.text: A trader who is net profitable over ten tracked practice trades is ready to trade real money
claims.note: Ten trades is far too small a sample to distinguish an edge from luck; statistical tests of trading skill need hundreds of trades.

claims.text: Gurus sell advice because it costs almost nothing to produce and its value can only be judged after payment
claims.note: Information goods have near-zero marginal cost and are credence goods, which economics identifies as a setting ripe for overpricing.

claims.text: Passive-income webinars use fake scarcity: pre-recorded presentations posing as live, countdown timers and limited slots
claims.note: Evergreen webinar software and false-urgency timers are standard in online course funnels and have featured in regulator complaints.

claims.text: Ghostwritten books on trending topics by non-experts are shallow and repetitive and mostly fail to sell
claims.note: Self-publishing platform data show most titles sell very few copies, though a minority of keyword-targeted books do earn steady royalties.

claims.text: Low-cost publishing schemes only pencil out by paying ghostwriters a fraction of professional rates
claims.note: At professional ghostwriting rates a short nonfiction book costs thousands, far above the expected royalties of a keyword-targeted title.

claims.text: Review swapping among course members to seed book reviews violates platform rules and risks account bans
claims.note: Major retailers prohibit reciprocal and incentivized reviews and have removed reviews and banned accounts for it.

claims.text: Course sellers often no longer use the method they sell, having pivoted to selling it once the opportunity closed
claims.note: A widely documented pattern across dropshipping, FBA and publishing gurus, though not every seller has abandoned the underlying business.

claims.text: Low-effort arbitrage pays only for early movers; once a method is widely taught, competition crowds out the returns
claims.note: Easily replicated strategies see returns compete away as entrants flood in, consistent with observed cycles in self-publishing and dropshipping niches.

claims.text: Framing failure as the student's fault for quitting shields the seller from criticism and exploits sunk-cost thinking
claims.note: A characterization of rhetorical strategy rather than a measurable outcome.

claims.text: The typical buyer of a passive-income course ends up net negative: out the course fee plus outsourcing costs, with no income
claims.note: Regulator cases and income disclosures for business-opportunity programs show most buyers earn little or nothing, though data specific to publishing courses is thin.

claims.text: Gurus inflate the stated value of bonuses so a multi-thousand-dollar course looks like a bargain
claims.note: Value stacking with arbitrary dollar figures is a standard course-funnel tactic with no independent basis for the stated values.

claims.text: Guru pitches push buyers to take on credit-card debt to pay for the course
claims.note: Consumer complaints and regulator actions against coaching programs repeatedly cite pressure to finance fees with credit.

claims.text: Courses that recruit their most successful students as paid coaches take on MLM-style recruitment dynamics
claims.note: Coach-recruitment tiers are common in coaching programs, but they lack the multi-level commission structure that defines an MLM.

claims.text: Small businesses will pay a recurring monthly fee for an AI phone agent because it replaces a salaried receptionist
claims.note: AI receptionists have a market, but most small businesses have no salaried receptionist to replace, and churn and bundled competition are unmeasured.

claims.text: Faceless AI-generated YouTube channels get buried by the algorithm and demonetized, so they rarely make money
claims.note: The platform tightened monetization rules against mass-produced and repetitive content, though some AI-assisted channels still earn.

claims.text: Anyone selling an AI trading bot is really selling a course, because a genuinely profitable bot would never be sold cheaply
claims.note: Profitable quantitative strategies decay when shared and firms that have them keep them proprietary; retail bot vendors mostly sell signals and courses.

claims.text: Businesses will pay substantial consulting fees to have someone audit where AI can save them time
claims.note: Demand for AI implementation help is real, but substantial fees go to credible consultants and most newcomers lack the track record.

claims.text: Generic AI copywriting and content-repurposing services have a short window because the tools are becoming self-serve
claims.note: Freelance-platform data show falling demand and rates for generic writing since 2023, though specialized niches persist.

claims.text: Selling qualified leads to businesses is the easiest AI service to sell because the value is immediately measurable
claims.note: Lead generation has clear measurable value, but it is crowded and disputes over lead quality are common, so easiest is overstated.

claims.text: Validate a service by pre-selling it and delivering manually before building any product
claims.note: Pre-selling and concierge delivery are well-supported lean-startup practices that reduce wasted build effort.

claims.text: Building custom AI agents for businesses is the biggest opportunity because it attacks their labor costs and few people can do it
claims.note: A forward-looking ranking by someone selling an agent platform; no independent data on agency-builder earnings exists yet.

claims.text: Most online advice on making money with AI comes from people who have not made money with AI
claims.note: An unverifiable characterization of other creators.

claims.text: Income reports published by passive-income bloggers include affiliate commissions on products recommended to readers
claims.note: Stated directly in the disclosure; affiliate revenue is a standard line in such reports.

claims.text: An experienced day trader can multiply a small account many times over within a month by trading momentum stocks.
claims.note: Among 1,551 persistent futures day traders the single best earned US$310 a day on average with a daily standard deviation of US$2,560, and only 0.5% beat a bank teller's wage; nobody shows multiplying an account in a month, though the setting is Brazilian index futures rather than momentum stocks.

claims.text: Beginner traders lose mainly by holding losing trades too long so average losses outgrow average wins.
claims.note: The disposition effect is well documented in retail trading data, but costs and lack of edge explain losses too.

claims.text: Commission-free brokerage increased retail trading frequency and volume.
claims.note: Elimination of commissions fuelled a retail participation boom and rise in day trading; retail options volume grew 143-224% from Nov 2019 to Jul 2021 (descriptive, not a causal test).

claims.text: Retail day traders have no edge trading large-cap stocks against high-frequency algorithms.
claims.note: Individuals' average daily loss is 19% higher when the HFT share of deals rises 10 points, and the authors conclude it is virtually impossible to compete with HFTs; the venue is index futures rather than large-cap stocks.

claims.text: Course and MLM sellers target stay-at-home mothers seeking flexible income.
claims.note: MLM participant surveys skew heavily toward women seeking flexible work, and the same demographic is targeted by creator-course marketing.

claims.text: In MLMs the product is incidental; the income pitch is the real product and recruitment saturates the market.
claims.note: Income disclosures and regulator analyses show most MLM participants lose money once recruitment saturates.

claims.text: Platform creator payouts are negligible for most creators even with large followings.
claims.note: Creator-economy surveys find median earnings from platform programs are tiny; meaningful income comes from brand deals or owned products.

claims.text: Producing polished short-form content takes hours per video and is effectively a full-time job.
claims.note: Creator time-use reports consistently show planning, filming and editing dominate, far beyond the posted runtime.

claims.text: Platforms push ordinary users into creator programs because free content benefits the platform.
claims.note: Platforms do onboard new accounts into creator and bonus programs; the incentive is clear even if the motive is inferred.

claims.text: Content about being a content creator attracts no audience; successful creators offer a specific subject or skill.
claims.note: Audience growth tracks a distinct topic or persona; meta-content about posting rarely builds a following.

claims.text: Brands now get user-generated ad content from small accounts for free product or nothing.
claims.note: UGC marketplaces and gifting-only campaigns are standard practice; pay is low or in-kind for small creators.

claims.text: A few percent per day compounds to impossible annual returns, so such claimed trading rates cannot be sustained.
claims.note: Compounding arithmetic; no documented investor has sustained anything close.

claims.text: A genuinely profitable short-term strategy is capacity-limited, so its owner would keep it secret rather than sell it.
claims.note: Quant funds routinely cap capacity and guard strategies; selling a capacity-limited edge destroys it, which makes advertised strategies suspect.

claims.text: Anyone with a trading audience can profit by selling into the buying their own stock calls trigger, a pump and dump.
claims.note: Regulators have charged influencers and newsletter operators for exactly this; event studies show audience-driven price spikes.

claims.text: Commission-free brokers sell order flow to market makers, so retail trades still carry a hidden cost.
claims.note: Wholesalers pay commission-free brokerages for the orders routed to them (payment for order flow), giving brokers an incentive to push trading in wider-spread assets; in Q2 2021 US brokerages received $284.4m of PFOF for stock orders and $581.2m for options.

claims.text: Leveraged options positions lose everything on modest adverse moves and can lose more than the amount invested.
claims.note: Bought options cap loss at the premium but expire worthless often; written or margined positions can exceed invested capital.

claims.text: Backtested candlestick patterns show no reliable edge.
claims.note: Academic tests of candlestick signals on major indices find no profitable predictive power after costs.

claims.text: Frequent trading incurs higher transaction costs and short-term tax rates than long-term investing.
claims.note: Trading costs more than triple day traders' losses, from 7 bps gross to 23.9 bps net per day; the tax-rate part of the claim is not examined.

claims.text: Quitting a job to trade costs lost wages and career progress on top of trading losses.
claims.note: Opportunity cost and resume gaps are real; most who try full-time trading return to employment.

claims.text: Even a world-class return on a small account earns less than a salary, so trading a small account as a primary income is a mistake.
claims.note: Top long-run investor records are around twenty percent a year; applied to typical retail capital that is below median wages.

claims.text: Dropshipping and marketplace reselling is ordinary retail competing with giants on thin margins.
claims.note: Marketplace sellers face fee stacks, price competition and platform control; survey data show most small sellers earn little.

claims.text: Starting or joining a startup is the most reliable way to get rich by compressing a career's work into a few years.
claims.note: Startups produce many self-made fortunes, but most fail and median founder and early-employee payoffs are near zero, so they are high-variance rather than reliable.

claims.text: Wealth is created by making things people want, not redistributed from a fixed pie.
claims.note: Long-run growth in real output is the standard evidence against zero-sum wealth.

claims.text: Getting rich requires work whose value is measured and decisions with leverage, which safe jobs lack.
claims.note: A useful framing consistent with where large fortunes arise, but it is a heuristic rather than a tested model.

claims.text: Startup payoffs are so skewed that the mean is large but the median is roughly zero.
claims.note: Venture return data show power-law outcomes with most companies returning nothing to founders.

claims.text: Big upside always comes with a real possibility of loss; a job that feels safe cannot make you rich.
claims.note: Risk-return trade-offs are general; counterexamples exist via long compounding of savings, so it is not absolute.

claims.text: Outsized financial success depends heavily on luck, which observers systematically underestimate.
claims.note: Studies of founder and investor outcomes show large unexplained variance and weak persistence, consistent with a big luck component.

claims.text: Developing a technique others can reuse gives leverage that one-customer-at-a-time service work lacks.
claims.note: Scalable products have near-zero marginal cost while services scale with hours; this is why software fortunes dwarf service ones.

claims.text: Number of users is the best measure of whether a startup has created wealth.
claims.note: Usage is a strong signal but can be bought or unmonetizable; revenue and retention matter too.

claims.text: Businesses built around what the founder enjoys are least likely to match what customers value.
claims.note: Passion-driven ventures often misjudge demand, though domain enthusiasm also drives persistence; evidence is mixed.

claims.text: Trying to capture market returns while avoiding their volatility through trading or leverage usually fails.
claims.note: Investor return-gap studies show timing and tactical strategies underperform buy-and-hold on average.

claims.text: Financial outcomes depend more on behavior such as saving and patience than on financial knowledge.
claims.note: Behavior-gap research supports it, but knowledge and income still matter; the examples given are anecdotes.

claims.text: Sustained moderate returns compounded for decades beat chasing the highest returns.
claims.note: Long-horizon wealth is dominated by time in market; high-return strategies tend to be unrepeatable or blow up.

claims.text: Visible luxury spending is evidence of money spent, not of wealth held.
claims.note: Millionaire-household studies show modest consumption; conspicuous spending correlates poorly with net worth.

claims.text: The finance industry attracts hucksters promising outsized returns, so too-good-to-be-true pitches usually are.
claims.note: Regulatory enforcement records show investment fraud consistently among the largest consumer-loss categories.

claims.text: Investment opportunity is inversely related to popularity, so crowded trades offer little upside.
claims.note: Valuation and flows evidence supports mean reversion of popular assets, but momentum can persist for long stretches.

claims.text: Long-term investors who follow short-term traders' price signals get hurt when the traders' game ends.
claims.note: Bubble episodes show late long-horizon buyers absorbing losses when momentum traders exit.

claims.text: Frequent tinkering with an investment plan interrupts compounding and lowers returns.
claims.note: Brokerage studies find the most active retail accounts underperform the least active after costs.

claims.text: Beginners with no experience can make real money with AI side hustles because the tools do the hard part.
claims.note: In a randomized trial of 640 Kenyan small-business owners given a GPT-4 business mentor, the average effect on revenue and profit was not distinguishable from zero and only above-median performers gained (about 15%), while below-median performers did nearly 10% worse: the tool did not do the hard part for the weakest operators (existing businesses in Kenya over two months, not beginners starting AI side hustles).

claims.text: Brands will pay for AI-generated UGC-style ad videos on monthly retainers.
claims.note: Some brands buy AI UGC creative, but many avoid synthetic-looking ads and retainers to individuals are unproven at scale.

claims.text: A beginner can sell small-business websites built with AI tools at prices comparable to freelance web designers.
claims.note: Small businesses can build basic sites themselves with the same tools, and beginners without a portfolio struggle to charge designer rates.

claims.text: Creators will pay a recurring fee for AI-assisted clipping of long-form content into shorts.
claims.note: Clipping services do sell to creators, but the work is commoditized and often paid per view rather than on retainer.

claims.text: AI-drafted digital products decouple income from hours because they sell repeatedly at zero marginal cost.
claims.note: Zero marginal cost is real, but most digital products sell very few copies and selling them takes ongoing hours of marketing.

claims.text: AI can replace subject expertise when creating an information product.
claims.note: Marketplaces are flooded with generic AI-written products, and buyers pay for trust and depth that expertise provides.

claims.text: Service-based side hustles tie income to hours worked, so they do not scale into passive income.
claims.note: Definitional for services; income stops when delivery stops unless a team is hired.

claims.text: Launching enough digital products guarantees an eventual hit.
claims.note: Repeated attempts raise the odds but guarantee nothing, and most sellers quit or run out of money before a hit.

claims.text: Most AI side hustles promoted online never earn their operator a dollar.
claims.note: Consistent with survey data on side-hustle earnings, though stated without evidence by a promoter of the remaining five.

claims.text: Any simple trading system stops working once it becomes widely known, because others arbitrage it away.
claims.note: Returns of 97 published stock-return predictors shrank 58% on average after publication, more for predictors built only from price and trading data, but the authors reject that predictability disappears entirely: widely known systems weaken rather than stop working.

claims.text: Profitable active trading is a full-time job needing research, data and infrastructure, not an evening hobby.
claims.note: Professional quant and discretionary shops run on teams and paid data; part-time retail traders underperform in brokerage studies.

claims.text: Guru pitches sell a single secret that replaces the sustained effort real trading requires.
claims.note: A description of marketing rhetoric rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: Correctly predicting a technology's success does not make buying its early companies profitable.
claims.note: Dot-com baskets bought in the late 1990s lost most of their value despite the internet succeeding; the same held for many crypto tokens.

claims.text: Speculative booms draw in young inexperienced traders who mistake the boom for insight.
claims.note: A 1% rise in Bitcoin price is followed by about a 1% rise in daily active crypto-app users (causal per the Kazakhstan price-shock event study), 40% of users are men under 35 vs 26% of the population, and young men are 1.5-3x more price-sensitive than older men or women, consistent with feedback trading; the paper infers but does not measure that entrants mistake the boom for insight.

claims.text: For most people, saving more and earning more at work moves wealth more than chasing investment returns.
claims.note: Retirement-adequacy research finds contribution rate and income dominate outcomes for typical households.

claims.text: A faceless YouTube channel can be built with free AI tools for scripts, voice and images at near-zero upfront cost.
claims.note: The production pipeline is genuinely cheap; the cost claim is about building, not earning.

claims.text: Faceless niches such as narrated stories, listicles and screen tutorials have proven audiences.
claims.note: Large faceless channels exist in each format; survivorship bias hides the many that got no views.

claims.text: Affiliate links let a channel earn before it meets platform monetization thresholds.
claims.note: Affiliate programs have no subscriber requirement; earnings still depend on views.

claims.text: Most new YouTube channels earn nothing for months and most starters quit before growth arrives.
claims.note: The vast majority of channels never reach monetization thresholds; early view counts are typically near zero.

claims.text: YouTube channel growth is driven by occasional breakout videos, so persistence matters more than any single upload.
claims.note: View distributions are heavy-tailed, but persistence alone does not produce a breakout without a resonant topic.

claims.text: YouTube ad revenue can become significant income once a channel is monetized.
claims.note: Most monetized channels earn little from ads, so significant income is the exception rather than what monetization typically brings.

claims.text: Assigning a purchase contract to an end buyer earns a wholesale fee without buying the property.
claims.note: Contract assignment is an established practice, though several states now require licensing or disclosure for it.

claims.text: Wholesaling needs almost no money because earnest deposits are small, refundable and can be borrowed.
claims.note: Deposits can be small, but finding discounted sellers takes paid data and marketing, and deposits are often at risk once contingencies lapse.

claims.text: In wholesaling, finding genuinely discounted sellers is the bottleneck; buyers are easy for a real deal.
claims.note: Cash-buyer demand for discounted property is deep; motivated-seller lead generation is the costly, competitive part.

claims.text: Direct-to-seller marketing costs money but yields larger wholesale spreads than sourcing from the MLS or other wholesalers.
claims.note: Removing intermediaries raises the spread per deal, but marketing cost per closed deal is substantial and rising with competition.

claims.text: Wholesale deal flow scales roughly linearly with outbound call volume at a given skill level.
claims.note: Volume raises deal count, but list quality and diminishing returns on the same leads make it sub-linear.

claims.text: A due-diligence clause lets a wholesaler cancel a contract and recover the deposit if no buyer appears.
claims.note: Standard contingency mechanics where sellers accept them; regulators object because sellers bear the cost of tied-up contracts.

claims.text: Most seller leads convert only after many follow-up contacts, so a CRM and persistent follow-up are essential.
claims.note: Multi-touch conversion is a general sales finding; the specific count is folklore.

claims.text: Meeting sellers in person yields better purchase prices than closing by phone.
claims.note: In-person rapport plausibly improves negotiation, but it is self-reported practice without controlled comparison.

claims.text: Bitcoin follows a four-year halving cycle with predictable peaks, year-long corrections and deep drawdowns
claims.note: Three past cycles loosely fit the pattern, which is too few to call peaks predictable, and ETF-era flows have already broken the timing.

claims.text: Crypto prices are driven by speculation and hype rather than underlying cash flows or fundamentals
claims.note: Most tokens have no earnings or claim on assets, and academic work finds crypto returns are explained mainly by momentum and attention rather than fundamentals.

claims.text: Dollar-cost averaging into a falling market beats trying to time the exact bottom
claims.note: DCA reliably avoids the timing problem but only pays off if the asset recovers; it does not reduce the risk that crypto stays down or goes to zero.

claims.text: Crypto positions can go to zero; it is a high-risk market where the upside does not come without the downside
claims.note: Thousands of tokens have gone to effectively zero and even large coins have had 80 percent drawdowns; the risk is well documented.

claims.text: Retail investors have a stronger edge in crypto than in stocks because they are not competing with institutions and insiders
claims.note: On-chain data show small holders (<1 BTC) buy as Bitcoin rises while whales and miners sell, so larger and more sophisticated investors profit at retail's expense even in calm periods, and 73-81% of retail entrants likely lost money; retail is the counterparty of insiders, not free of them.

claims.text: Identifying crypto narratives early (AI agents, meme coins, new chains) is how investors capture outsized returns
claims.note: The winning examples are survivorship-selected; most narrative and meme tokens lose most of their value and retail buyers rarely get in early.

claims.text: Buying the dip only works in an uptrending market; in a downtrend dip-buying loses money
claims.note: Trend-following has some empirical support, but defining the trend is only clear in hindsight, so the rule is hard to act on in real time.

claims.text: A few large winners in a diversified speculative portfolio make up for many losing positions
claims.note: Power-law portfolios do work this way when a big winner is held, but most retail speculative crypto portfolios underperform simply holding the leading asset.

claims.text: Interest-rate cuts are liquidity events that flow into crypto and start rallies
claims.note: Crypto prices have moved with easy-money conditions since 2020, but the link is loose and lagged and cuts have not reliably started rallies.

claims.text: AI agents will soon help individual traders earn more than professional fund managers
claims.note: No independent evidence exists that retail AI trading agents beat professionals; the same tools are available to institutions with more data and capital.

claims.text: MLM income comes mainly from recruiting and leading a downline, not from selling product to retail customers
claims.note: All 30 MLMs with earnings data (and all 350 whose compensation plans Taylor reviewed) pay rewards primarily for recruiting a large downline, not for retailing products, with most payout going to the highest levels.

claims.text: MLM product margins are too thin for a distributor to build a large business on them
claims.note: Per-unit margins are modest after required purchases and upline cuts, but the bigger problem is that most distributors sell little product at all.

claims.text: An MLM distributorship is not the distributor's own business; the company can terminate it at any time without cause
claims.note: Standard MLM distributor agreements include at-will termination and the company owns the customer and downline data.

claims.text: Building your own email list and audience before promoting an MLM protects your income from comp-plan changes or termination
claims.note: Owning an audience does reduce dependence on one vendor, but it mostly shifts the business to selling courses and books rather than making the MLM itself pay.

claims.text: People who need money are the worst MLM recruits; those who do not need it succeed
claims.note: Recruits with existing networks and capital do outperform, but the claim mostly describes who survives the attrition rather than a mechanism that helps recruits.

claims.text: Anyone can reach several thousand dollars a month of passive cash flow within a year if they decide to
claims.note: MLM income disclosures and small-business survival data show the large majority of people who try earn little or nothing in the first year.

claims.text: A recurring passive income stream is financially equivalent to a lump sum invested at a fixed yield
claims.note: The arithmetic holds but the equivalence ignores that business cash flow is riskier, less durable and less transferable than invested capital.

claims.text: Publishing a book or course makes you an authority that prospects say yes to before hearing the offer
claims.note: Authority signals help conversion modestly, but most self-published books and courses reach few readers and do not presell prospects.

claims.text: People fail to get rich because they never do the math on what it takes, not because it is hard
claims.note: This is a motivational framing; goal arithmetic is trivial and the difficulty lies in customer acquisition and retention, which the framing waves away.

claims.text: Most ecommerce side-hustle failures come from poor execution, not from a broken business model
claims.note: Rising ad costs, copycat competition and thin margins are structural and sink well-executed stores too.

claims.text: Dropshipping needs no upfront inventory because the customer pays before the seller orders from the supplier
claims.note: The customer pays before the seller orders from the supplier, so no inventory is bought up front, though ads and tools still cost money.

claims.text: Product research tools showing live sales data let you validate demand before spending on ads
claims.note: These tools show that demand exists, but every subscriber sees the same products and existing sales do not predict a new store's conversion or ad cost.

claims.text: Slow or unreliable supplier fulfillment kills dropshipping stores through refunds and chargebacks
claims.note: Long shipping times are the main driver of dropshipping disputes and payment-processor holds, which is well documented by platforms and sellers.

claims.text: Visitors judge a store's trustworthiness within seconds, so generic-looking stores lose sales before the copy is read
claims.note: Web credibility research supports fast first impressions, but the effect size on conversion for dropshipping stores is not independently measured.

claims.text: Finding a winning ad requires testing many creatives and angles at once; a single ad almost never succeeds
claims.note: Creative testing is standard practice and improves odds, but it multiplies the budget required and most tests still lose money.

claims.text: AI-generated avatar videos can replace hiring real creators for UGC-style ads
claims.note: AI avatars produce cheap usable ad variants, but there is no independent evidence they convert like real creators and synthetic testimonials raise platform and consumer-protection issues.

claims.text: Leaving detailed ad targeting blank lets the ad platform's algorithm find buyers better than manual targeting
claims.note: Broad targeting is the platform's own recommendation and works for conversion-optimised campaigns with enough budget, but small accounts often lack the data for it to learn.

claims.text: Paid-ad dropshipping is only profitable when revenue per ad dollar clears product cost, fees and shipping
claims.note: Return on ad spend must exceed the inverse of the margin after goods and fees; this is basic unit economics.

claims.text: Students of dropshipping coaching programs collectively generate tens of millions in sales
claims.note: Empire consistently claimed hundreds of clients generating over $150 million in revenue; the FTC alleges this was false and most clients lost money, so this type of aggregate-sales claim was fabricated in at least this case.

claims.text: Amazon's fulfillment and referral fees take a large share of an FBA seller's profit
claims.note: Combined referral, fulfillment and storage fees commonly take 30 to 50 percent of the sale price, per Amazon's own fee schedules.

claims.text: Retail and online arbitrage needs the least capital but cannot scale into a business because supply is capped by store purchase limits
claims.note: Clearance deals are one-off and retailers cap quantities, so arbitrage income is irregular and labour-intensive; this is widely acknowledged even by its promoters.

claims.text: Wholesale reselling of branded products on Amazon needs no ads because demand already exists on the listing
claims.note: Demand on existing listings is real, but brand gating and buy-box competition with other resellers squeeze margins on popular items.

claims.text: Private-label Amazon selling requires thousands in upfront capital plus ad spend and a long learning curve
claims.note: Minimum order quantities, barcodes, trademarks, photography and launch advertising routinely cost several thousand before the first sale.

claims.text: Third-party sellers cannot win listings where Amazon itself sells, because Amazon undercuts on price and holds the buy box
claims.note: Amazon retail has structural cost advantages and the buy-box algorithm favours price, so competing on its own listings is a well-known losing proposition.

claims.text: Selling on another brand's private-label listing invites complaints that get a seller's account suspended
claims.note: Brand registry lets owners report unauthorised sellers and repeated complaints do lead to suspensions, though a single instance usually does not.

claims.text: Sales tax or VAT charged on Amazon's fees is a hidden cost that the fee calculator understates for unregistered sellers
claims.note: In the UK and EU, Amazon adds VAT to seller fees for non-VAT-registered sellers who cannot reclaim it, which reduces the net margin shown.

claims.text: A first wholesale order should be a small test batch to avoid being stuck with unsellable inventory
claims.note: Small test orders limit downside from gating, undercutting or slow sales; it is standard inventory risk management.

claims.text: With personal coaching a beginner can build a six-figure Amazon business within a year
claims.note: Automators' $5,000 one-on-one Amazon coaching advertised students making $10,000+ a month, but the FTC alleges virtually none of its coaching clients made the advertised amounts and most did not recoup their investment.

claims.text: Households that repeatedly chase get-rich-quick schemes end up with more debt rather than more wealth
claims.note: Each scheme carries upfront costs and most lose money, so the pattern compounds into debt; this is consistent with consumer-finance research on scheme victims.

claims.text: Credit-card rewards points are never worth carrying interest-bearing debt to earn
claims.note: Points are worth about a cent each while revolving interest runs 20 to 30 percent a year, so any carried balance wipes out the rewards many times over.

claims.text: Rotating debt through 0% balance-transfer offers is a gimmick that delays rather than solves overspending
claims.note: Transfers carry fees and promotional rates expire; research on balance-transfer users shows many end up with the same or larger balances.

claims.text: Timeshares are a financial scheme that leaves buyers worse off and hard to exit
claims.note: Timeshares depreciate immediately, carry rising maintenance fees and have almost no resale market; consumer regulators treat exit scams as a direct consequence.

claims.text: Ordinary people have little chance of out-gaming banks and credit-card companies at their own products
claims.note: Card issuers design rewards and promotional offers around revolver behaviour; their profitability depends on most customers not winning the game.

claims.text: Compulsive spending is emotionally driven and needs skills or therapy, not budgeting tips
claims.note: Compulsive buying is a recognised behavioural pattern with evidence for cognitive-behavioural treatment, though structural changes to accounts also help.

claims.text: A primary residence is not an asset because it does not produce cash flow
claims.note: A house is an asset by any accounting definition; the cash-flow framing is a redefinition, though it correctly warns that an owner-occupied home costs money rather than paying it.

claims.text: Saving cash is a losing strategy because fiat money has lost value since leaving the gold standard
claims.note: Inflation erodes idle cash, but an emergency fund and a high savings rate are among the strongest predictors of household wealth.

claims.text: Using bank debt to buy cash-flowing rental property is how ordinary people become rich
claims.note: Leveraged rentals built some fortunes, but most ordinary households build wealth through home equity and retirement savings, and leverage magnifies losses.

claims.text: Schools teach nothing about money and teachers are poor, so formal education is the wrong place to learn wealth
claims.note: Personal-finance education is thin in most curricula, but educational attainment remains one of the strongest predictors of lifetime income and wealth.

claims.text: A rental property that does not cash-flow from day one should not be bought; promises it will pay later are a trap
claims.note: Negative-cash-flow 'value-add' deals do fail often, but renovation plays can work when underwritten carefully; the rule is conservative rather than universal.

claims.text: Raising your failure rate (more sales calls, more attempts) is how people learn to sell and succeed
claims.note: The model's individual-level lesson is that since lucky events cannot be controlled, the best strategy at any talent level is to broaden activity and output to maximise exposure to lucky events; it does not model learning from failure.

claims.text: Hands-on simulation games teach accounting and investing better than lectures
claims.note: Active learning generally beats lectures in education research, but there is no independent evidence that board-game simulations improve real financial outcomes.

claims.text: A large rental property portfolio produces monthly cash flow far exceeding a salary
claims.note: A large paid-down portfolio can out-earn a salary, but leveraged portfolios often cash-flow thinly and reaching that size takes decades of capital and risk.

claims.text: A from-scratch dropshipping store can get its first sales within hours of launching ads
claims.note: Fast first sales happen when copying a product with proven ads, but they are often loss-making and say nothing about sustained profit.

claims.text: A one-week dropshipping test with a few hundred dollars ends close to break-even after ads, goods and fees
claims.note: First-hand tests consistently show ad spend consuming most revenue; the net result is typically a small profit or loss.

claims.text: Copying a proven competitor's product, page and ad angles is the fastest route to first sales
claims.note: Cloning validated offers does shortcut discovery, but it puts the copier in direct ad-auction competition with the original and fuels the race to the bottom.

claims.text: Cheap static image ads can outperform produced UGC video ads for the same product
claims.note: Creative performance is product- and audience-specific; a one-day comparison on tiny spend is noise, though statics do sometimes win.

claims.text: Ad-platform attribution misses some purchases, so dashboard numbers understate true results
claims.note: Post-privacy-change attribution loss on Meta is well documented; advertisers routinely reconcile against store orders.

claims.text: Personalised low-cost jewelry sells at many times unit cost because of high perceived value
claims.note: Markups on personalised jewelry are wide, but customer acquisition cost absorbs most of the spread.

claims.text: Engaging with sponsored posts trains social feeds to surface products other sellers are advertising, replacing paid research tools
claims.note: Feed algorithms do respond to ad engagement, so this surfaces active campaigns; it shows what is being advertised, not what is profitable.

claims.text: Reaching profitability requires more creative tests and ad budget than a beginner's small budget allows
claims.note: Testing enough creatives to find a winner typically costs more than the few hundred dollars beginners are told they need.

claims.text: Online side hustles fail without an owned audience because traffic is the real bottleneck
claims.note: Customer acquisition is the dominant cost in online business, but many profitable stores run on paid traffic without an audience; the audience framing suits a YouTube coach.

claims.text: Paid-traffic dropshipping margins collapse as ad costs rise and competitors copy the product
claims.note: Low barriers to entry mean any winning product is cloned within weeks, and ad auctions price the margin away; this is the standard dropshipping failure mode.

claims.text: Running a marketing agency for local businesses is a full-time job whose income stops when outreach stops, not a passive side hustle
claims.note: Agency work is client services with ongoing delivery and churn; it is a legitimate business but has none of the passive-income properties pitched.

claims.text: Flipping products, websites or domains only works when the market already wants the item; results are mostly timing and luck
claims.note: Resale depends on existing demand and skilled flippers do develop an edge, but for beginners outcomes are dominated by timing.

claims.text: A small channel in a high-value niche can out-earn a large general-audience channel because revenue is views times value per viewer
claims.note: Revenue per view varies many-fold by niche, so this can happen, but the cited figures are selected anecdotes.

claims.text: AI script writing removes the main barrier that stops beginners from starting a YouTube channel
claims.note: Discoverability and retention, not scripts, are the binding constraints, and AI lowers the scripting barrier for every competitor equally.

claims.text: A digital product built once earns passive income for years while you sleep
claims.note: Most digital products sell almost nothing without continual promotion, so passive income for years is the rare case.

claims.text: YouTube income compounds because old videos keep generating views and sales years later
claims.note: Evergreen search-driven videos do keep earning, but most videos decay quickly, so compounding holds only for a minority of channels.

claims.text: Most prediction-market users lose money; winnings concentrate in a small number of sophisticated accounts
claims.note: On-chain analyses show a large majority of accounts are net losers with profits concentrated in a few hundred wallets, matching sportsbook and retail-trading patterns.

claims.text: By labelling bets as event contracts, prediction markets operate where gambling is illegal and avoid state taxes and age limits
claims.note: Federal commodity-exchange registration is the stated basis for operating nationally; multiple states are suing on exactly this point.

claims.text: Prediction-market odds forecast about as well as professional forecasters on economic questions but have notable big misses
claims.note: Studies find calibration comparable to experts on liquid macro markets, with thin markets and low-volume events showing large errors.

claims.text: The bulk of prediction-market volume is sports betting rather than hedging real-life risks
claims.note: Platform volume data show sports contracts dominate; the risk-hedging use case is a small share.

claims.text: Crowds with money at stake produce forecasts that outperform polls
claims.note: Election markets have matched or modestly beaten polls on average, but the edge is small and fails in thin or manipulable markets.

claims.text: Influencer posts showing easy prediction-market winnings are often undisclosed paid promotions
claims.note: The segment confirmed one paid post; the broader pattern matches documented undisclosed promotion in sports betting and crypto.

claims.text: Regulators are not enforcing existing authority to block event contracts on war, terrorism and assassination
claims.note: Such contracts are live on major platforms despite statutory authority to prohibit them; the regulator has instead sued states that tried to intervene.

claims.text: Day trading lets a small account earn in a single day what long-term investing earns in a year on the same risk
claims.note: Persistent futures day traders had negative expected daily profit (mean -US$48.81, 97% losing) with large volatility, the opposite of earning a year's investment return in a day at equal risk.

claims.text: Trading psychology, especially accepting losses, is the main determinant of trading success
claims.note: Behavioural biases do hurt traders, but no amount of discipline creates an edge where none exists; psychology explains failure more than it produces success.

claims.text: Technical patterns such as Fibonacci retracements and fair value gaps predict where price will react
claims.note: Academic tests of Fibonacci and similar chart levels find no predictive power beyond chance; the golden-ratio-in-nature justification is numerology.

claims.text: Leverage lets a small account take large positions while keeping the dollar amount at risk fixed
claims.note: ESMA: leverage raises the probability of a larger loss more than of a larger gain, automatic margin close-out reduces but does not eliminate the risk of losing all or more than the initial margin, and in gapping markets the investor may be unable to close at their preferred price, so the amount at risk is not fixed.

claims.text: Funded-trader (prop firm) accounts let beginners trade size without their own capital
claims.note: Most evaluation-based prop firm customers fail and pay repeated fees, and few beginners ever trade funded size or get paid.

claims.text: Proprietary buy/sell indicators reliably flag over- and undervalued zones to trade
claims.note: Oscillator-style indicators are lagging transforms of price; no independent evidence shows paid indicator suites produce an edge after costs.

claims.text: Exponential recruiting exhausts the population within a dozen or so cycles, so most MLM participants are structurally at the bottom
claims.note: In nearly every rank-based disclosure the vast majority of participants sit in the two or three lowest ranks (one example: 92.37% in the bottom rank averaging $41.69, top ranks fractions of a percent), confirming most are structurally at the bottom; the report does not test the exponential-exhaustion arithmetic.

claims.text: Most MLM participants earn little or nothing and a substantial share lose money
claims.note: Of the 601 surveyed participants, 25% made any profit over their whole time in the MLM: 14% under $5,000, 6% $5,000 to $9,999, 3% $10,000 to $24,999, 3% $25,000 or more, and 3 people (0.5%) $100,000 or more; 47% lost money (41% under $5,000, 3% $5,000 to $9,999, 1% over $10,000) and 27% broke even; all self-reported.

claims.text: Volume-based discounts and rank requirements push distributors to buy product they cannot sell
claims.note: Inventory loading is a documented feature of many compensation plans and was central to the regulator's complaint cited in the segment.

claims.text: MLM distributors make unsubstantiated health claims to move product
claims.note: Undercover recordings and regulator warning letters repeatedly document disease-cure claims by distributors despite company policies.

claims.text: MLM compensation plans are deliberately convoluted, obscuring how money is actually made
claims.note: Plans are demonstrably complex and hard for participants to model; whether the complexity is deliberate is inferred rather than shown.

claims.text: MLM buyback policies for unsold inventory are partial or require the distributor to resign
claims.note: Typical buyback terms deduct restocking fees and apply only on termination, which company policies state.

claims.text: Regulators rarely bring pyramid-scheme cases against MLMs because the industry is opaque and politically connected
claims.note: The count of enforcement actions is low relative to the industry's size and a congressional direct-selling caucus exists.

claims.text: MLM income disclosures count only active distributors, overstating the share of all participants who earn anything
claims.note: Of 70 disclosures only 11 clearly include all participants; 29 drop everyone who earned no commission and 24 drop participants the MLM deems 'inactive', so at least 75% present a distribution that omits zero-earners.

claims.text: Starting a business with no money is a competitive advantage because well-funded founders lose imagination and discipline
claims.note: Family income is a powerful predictor of becoming an incorporated entrepreneur: a $100,000 higher 1979 family income is associated with an almost 60% higher probability of incorporation after controlling for ability, traits and education, which the authors read as credit constraints materially hindering entrepreneurship; the paper tests entry rather than founder discipline, but points the opposite way to the claim.

claims.text: The idea that paying for a course makes you act on it is a sales pitch; personal pain, not payment, drives follow-through
claims.note: Course completion rates are very low regardless of price, which undercuts the pay-to-pay-attention line used to sell coaching.

claims.text: Business ideas are worthless on their own; execution is where the value lies, so NDAs are pointless
claims.note: Investor and founder consensus holds that execution dominates, though some ideas have genuine defensible value and NDAs matter in specific technical contexts.

claims.text: Businesses that rise fast fall fast; durable companies take many years to build
claims.note: Rapid growth without systems does correlate with collapse, but many durable companies also grew fast; the rule is a heuristic, not a law.

claims.text: Public stock investing is a scam because the investor cannot control the outcome
claims.note: Diversified index investing has delivered positive real returns over every long period on record; lack of control is not fraud.

claims.text: Looking after a few existing customers grows a business faster than chasing new ones
claims.note: Retention is cheaper than acquisition and referrals compound, but a three-customer business is fragile to losing any one of them.

claims.text: Ventures with co-founders and employee equity succeed where solo ventures fail
claims.note: Startup studies find mixed results: co-founded companies raise more and grow faster, but solo founders have comparable survival in some datasets.

claims.text: Income from dividends or interest large enough to matter requires a capital base most beginners lack
claims.note: At typical 2-4% yields, a modest weekly income needs six figures invested, as the video's own arithmetic shows.

claims.text: Companies with long dividend-growth records are safer income picks than those offering very high yields
claims.note: Very high yields often precede cuts and dividend-growth stocks have had lower volatility, but a long record does not guarantee future payouts.

claims.text: A digital product priced modestly needs only a few sales a week to become an easy income
claims.note: The arithmetic works, but most self-published digital products sell close to nothing, so a few sales a week is not easy.

claims.text: Content creators whose content is good and algorithm-friendly will succeed; luck is no longer the main factor
claims.note: Experiments on cultural markets show large randomness in outcomes at similar quality, and most channels never reach monetization.

claims.text: Angel investing returns come from a few winners offsetting many losses
claims.note: Angel and venture return data are heavily skewed, with most deals losing money and a few producing the portfolio's return.

claims.text: Affiliate marketing needs no special skills or experience to earn a full-time income
claims.note: Affiliate income depends on building an audience or search traffic, which is a skilled, slow process; most affiliates earn little.

claims.text: Renting out assets you already own, like a driveway or spare room, produces modest income with little effort
claims.note: Peer-to-peer rental platforms do pay owners, though income depends heavily on location and demand.

claims.text: Peer-to-peer lending reliably gives retail lenders a positive return
claims.note: Diversified lenders on major platforms mostly earned positive returns, but defaults and platform failures left many retail lenders with losses.

claims.text: Rewriting resumes with AI can be sold as a service for hundreds of dollars each
claims.note: Paid resume writing is a real market, but it is crowded and commoditized and beginners selling AI rewrites rarely command the top-end prices.

claims.text: Writing YouTube scripts with AI for other creators pays a reliable freelance income
claims.note: Scriptwriting gigs exist, but freelance platforms are crowded, creators increasingly use AI themselves, and income for beginners is irregular rather than reliable.

claims.text: Uploading self-published books to Amazon produces ongoing royalties with little further work
claims.note: The median self-published title earns almost nothing and the store is flooded with low-content books, so ongoing royalties with little work is not the typical result.

claims.text: Anyone who can talk to an AI can build and sell a software app without coding
claims.note: AI builders make prototypes, but reliable sellable software and finding paying users remain out of reach for most non-coders.

claims.text: Paid coaching gives a better return than a college degree
claims.note: The college wage premium is large and well measured, while coaching returns rest on self-reported, selected testimonials.

claims.text: Luxury lifestyles displayed by gurus can be rented or faked
claims.note: Rented cars, houses and jets are documented in exposes of course sellers; the display proves nothing about income.

claims.text: People selling courses about a money-making method earn more from the courses than from the method
claims.note: Several course sellers have disclosed that course revenue exceeded their business revenue, and regulators have made the same finding.

claims.text: Dropshipping is a real business needing marketing and operations skills, not an easy money method
claims.note: Fulfillment is outsourced but customer acquisition, support and competition are the same as for any retailer.

claims.text: Affiliate commissions bias online reviews of courses toward positive ratings
claims.note: Commissioned reviewers face a clear conflict of interest, and referral programs are a standard course-marketing tactic.

claims.text: Guru income figures are revenue before ad and product costs, and screenshots can be edited
claims.note: Sales dashboards show gross revenue; profit after ads is typically a fraction, and fabricated screenshots are documented.

claims.text: Most of what paid online courses teach is available free online
claims.note: Platform docs, free guides and videos cover the same material; the course adds structure, not secrets.

claims.text: Costly mistakes are an unavoidable part of learning an online business
claims.note: A framing about learning, not a measurable prediction.

claims.text: AI tools can build a dropshipping store, product pages and ads in hours instead of days
claims.note: Store builders, copy and image generators do produce a functional store quickly; whether it sells is a separate question.

claims.text: A dropshipping store that barely breaks even in its first week can be optimized into steady monthly profit
claims.note: A prediction with no follow-up; some stores improve with optimization, most are abandoned.

claims.text: Low barrier to entry means dropshippers compete with many stores selling identical products from the same suppliers
claims.note: Same catalog and same suppliers, so price and ad competition is structural.

claims.text: It takes about a year of full-time work for dropshipping to replace an average income
claims.note: Plausible for those who succeed, but there is no independent data and most stores never get there.

claims.text: Most new businesses, including online stores, fail within a few years
claims.note: Of US private establishments opened in the year to March 2015, 79.6% survived one year, 61.4% three years, 50.2% five years and 34.7% ten years (other cohorts are similar), so about half close within five years and two-thirds within ten; 'most fail within a few years' overstates it, establishment exits include sales and relocations rather than only failures, and there is no online-store breakdown.

claims.text: Shoppers increasingly recognize dropshipped goods and buy them cheaper direct from Temu or AliExpress
claims.note: Reverse image search and direct-from-China marketplaces have compressed resale margins on generic goods.

claims.text: A distinct brand identity is required to succeed in dropshipping today
claims.note: Branding helps differentiate identical goods, but it is not sufficient and some generic stores still profit short-term.

claims.text: Confident experts offering formulas forecast worse than cautious ones
claims.note: Tetlock's long-run forecasting study found hedgehog-style confident experts less accurate than fox-style ones.

claims.text: The least competent are the most confident, so the loudest advice tends to be the least informed
claims.note: Dunning-Kruger overconfidence partly replicates but much of the effect is statistical regression; it does not show loud advisers are wrong.

claims.text: Successful people cannot see their own luck and retroactively construct a merit narrative
claims.note: Hindsight bias and confabulation are documented, but it is not shown that success stories are mostly rationalization.

claims.text: Success-advice media profits from keeping its audience anxious and unsuccessful
claims.note: An argument about incentives and intent, not a measurable claim.

claims.text: Subleasing a landlord's property and listing it short-term lets you run rentals without buying property
claims.note: The arbitrage model exists and is used, subject to lease consent and local short-term-rental rules.

claims.text: Landlords will agree to short-term-rental subleasing if offered a rent bonus and professional cleaning
claims.note: Most landlords refuse subleasing on lease, insurance and building-rule grounds, and a small bonus rarely changes that.

claims.text: A sublet short-term rental only cash-flows if revenue is a multiple of the rent, not merely above it
claims.note: Cleaning, utilities, platform fees, furniture amortization and vacancy mean revenue near rent is a loss.

claims.text: Furnishing and launching an arbitraged short-term rental needs five figures of upfront cash
claims.note: Deposit, first rent, furniture and setup consistently reach that range in operator reports.

claims.text: One arbitraged short-term rental unit nets a couple of thousand dollars a month once set up
claims.note: Market data show falling revenue per listing and many arbitraged units earning below rent and costs, so a couple of thousand net is not typical.

claims.text: A running short-term rental needs only about an hour a week of the operator's time
claims.note: Guest messaging, turnover coordination, maintenance and reviews take far more unless a paid manager is hired, which cuts profit.

claims.text: Short-term rental arbitrage scales linearly by adding units
claims.note: Each unit needs fresh capital, a willing landlord and more management, and regulation caps many markets, so linear scaling is a best case.

claims.text: Futures let small accounts day trade without the pattern-day-trader minimum that applies to stocks
claims.note: The PDT rule covers margin stock and option accounts; futures accounts are exempt, though margin and leverage risks apply.

claims.text: Prop-firm evaluation challenges are structured so most participants pay fees and never get funded
claims.note: Firms' own and regulator disclosures show low pass rates and fee-driven revenue; some firms have been sanctioned.

claims.text: Trading fewer, higher-quality setups beats frequent trading because fees and fatigue erode returns
claims.note: Brokerage data show the most active retail traders underperform the least active.

claims.text: Support and resistance levels tested many times are more reliable
claims.note: Some evidence of clustering at round numbers and prior extremes, but technical levels have weak predictive power out of sample.

claims.text: A stock trading above VWAP is intraday bullish and below VWAP bearish
claims.note: VWAP describes the day's average fill; it is widely watched but has little documented edge as a signal.

claims.text: Buying pullbacks to VWAP on gapped-up large caps is a profitable beginner strategy
claims.note: Intraday momentum effects exist in some studies but there is no independent evidence this setup beats costs for retail traders.

claims.text: Becoming consistently profitable at day trading takes years, so keep a day job meanwhile
claims.note: Panel regressions on 1,551 traders with 300+ trading days find no learning: expected profit stays negative and does not improve with time, so keeping a day job is supported but years of practice do not reliably bring profitability.

claims.text: Course coaches often have no verifiable track record in the business they teach
claims.note: Documented cases are common but not universal; some course sellers do run real operating businesses.
