claims.text: Monetization-focused creator courses steer students toward product-review and affiliate content
claims.note: Observed in several reviewed courses, but it is one reviewer's sample.

claims.text: Faceless YouTube channels earning tens of thousands a month are possible but improbable for most
claims.note: Partner-program thresholds and typical CPMs mean most channels never reach that; a few outliers do.

claims.text: Fast-monetization methods sold in faceless-YouTube courses violate platform terms and risk demonetization
claims.note: Buying subscribers and watch time breaches partner-program rules and triggers removal.

claims.text: The faceless-channel playbook is to copy already-viral videos, which the platform rewards
claims.note: Derivative formats do spread, but duplicative and mass-produced AI content is now explicitly demonetized.

claims.text: Channels run on paid scripts, voiceovers and editors often run out of money before monetization
claims.note: Per-video costs with no revenue for months is the standard failure mode; abandoned channels are visible everywhere.

claims.text: Platform rule changes can demonetize a channel at any time, so creators need other income streams
claims.note: Repeated policy changes and mass demonetizations are documented; diversification is standard advice.

claims.text: Course sellers advertise niches they do not use to keep competition out of their own
claims.note: Plausible incentive but no evidence beyond anecdote.

claims.text: Get-rich-quick promoters hop between fads and rarely sustain a business
claims.note: Fad-hopping is observable, but the survival rate of these promoters has not been measured.

claims.text: Demeaning salaried jobs and college is a sales tactic; both generally improve financial outcomes
claims.note: The college earnings premium and the stability of salaried work are well documented, though college is not right for everyone.

claims.text: Success depends more on a support system, coachability and consistency than on the perfect program
claims.note: Motivational framing; the components are not operationalized.

claims.text: Winning dropshipping products are trending, hard to find in stores, and solve a real problem
claims.note: Reasonable heuristics, but trending products are also the most copied, so the criteria do not secure margin.

claims.text: An AI chatbot can validate a product's market potential before spending on ads
claims.note: A chatbot can summarize public signals but cannot measure conversion rates or ad costs, so it cannot validate whether a product will sell profitably.

claims.text: Reusing other people's video ads risks account bans and competes with identical creatives
claims.note: Copyright and ad-policy enforcement is real, and duplicate creatives fatigue faster.

claims.text: Buyers of paid ecommerce coaching are much more likely to succeed than people using free content
claims.note: Success rates come from vendor testimonials, and regulators have found most buyers of such coaching do not recoup their fees.

claims.text: Affiliate marketing and dropshipping are so saturated that newcomers rarely make money
claims.note: Both still produce income for some, but saturation and rising ad costs have cut newcomer odds; 'don't work' overstates it.

claims.text: NFT flipping and crypto trading lose money for most participants
claims.note: Post-2022 NFT collections are mostly worthless and retail crypto trading studies show majority losses.

claims.text: AI has eliminated low-level freelance work like captioning and data entry
claims.note: Platform demand for transcription and basic data entry has collapsed; some human QA work remains.

claims.text: Print-on-demand is overcrowded with sellers offering identical products
claims.note: Marketplace listing counts and seller reports show saturation in mainstream niches.

claims.text: Selling outcome-based retainers instead of hourly time is how service income scales
claims.note: Retainers do stabilize income, but outcome pricing shifts risk to the seller and needs a track record.

claims.text: Switching ideas every few weeks is the main reason online businesses fail
claims.note: Persistence matters, but many ventures fail on unit economics regardless of focus.

claims.text: Buying a boring small business and automating it with AI yields strong returns
claims.note: Small-business acquisition can pay off with capital and operating skill, but many acquisitions underperform and AI gains are anecdotal.

claims.text: Word-search puzzle books sell well on KDP because few sellers can make them
claims.note: Free puzzle generators are widely available and the category is saturated with near-identical listings, so the premise of few sellers is false.

claims.text: Print-on-demand t-shirts on Amazon earn passive income if you find small untapped niches
claims.note: Tier limits, saturation and takedowns keep typical print-on-demand royalties small, and untapped niches close fast once found.

claims.text: Video reviews with affiliate links convert better than written blog reviews
claims.note: Video can build trust and reach, but written search content still converts well for purchase-intent queries and there is no clear independent comparison.

claims.text: Educational YouTube content earns higher ad rates than entertainment content
claims.note: Finance, business and education niches report RPMs several times those of entertainment.

claims.text: Commission-only sales pays for results not hours, so income is uncapped but can be zero for months
claims.note: That is how commission compensation works; agent income distributions are highly skewed.

claims.text: Rental property bought cheaply produces monthly cash flow independent of your labor
claims.note: Net rental yields after expenses averaged 6.1% in the lowest-price-tier cities against 2.4% in the highest, so cheaper rentals do produce more income per dollar, but the figures are index-level after paying for management, repairs and vacancy, and say nothing about the owner's labour.

claims.text: YouTube ad revenue can reach five figures a month for a channel in a high-paying niche
claims.note: Finance channels with large audiences do report this; it is the top tail, not the norm.

claims.text: Tenant rent paying down a mortgage is income even though it is not cash
claims.note: Principal paydown builds equity and is effectively taxed because principal is not deductible, but it is illiquid and can be lost to price falls.

claims.text: Several independent income sources reduce the risk of any one failing
claims.note: Diversification reduces income variance as long as the sources are not correlated.

claims.text: Amazon FBA is saturated and generic private-label of Alibaba goods no longer works
claims.note: Seller counts, fee increases and Chinese direct sellers have compressed margins on undifferentiated goods.

claims.text: An established FBA business runs on a few hours a week of the owner's time
claims.note: Possible with paid staff and a mature product, but most sellers report more hands-on time and the setup labor is excluded.

claims.text: Retail arbitrage and wholesale on Amazon are low-margin, labor-intensive and get cut out by suppliers
claims.note: Both models are widely reported as thin-margin and vulnerable to brand gating and supplier disintermediation.

claims.text: A product branded for a specific niche community can still succeed on Amazon
claims.note: Niche branding is a real differentiator and 'can' is modest, but most new Amazon private-label products fail to reach profitability and niche wins attract copycats.

claims.text: Cross-selling on TikTok Shop creates a flywheel that lifts Amazon rank and sales
claims.note: External traffic does lift Amazon rank, but the self-reinforcing loop only appears when a product catches on with creators, which most do not.

claims.text: Chinese sellers and tariffs are not a real threat to a well-branded consumable product
claims.note: China-based sellers now hold a large share of Amazon marketplace listings and tariff changes have squeezed many FBA margins, so the threat is real even for branded consumables.

claims.text: Committing fully with no plan B is the key to success in network marketing
claims.note: Commitment does not change the structural payout; income disclosures show nearly all participants lose regardless of effort.

claims.text: If someone in your company reached the top, you can too regardless of background
claims.note: 64 of 70 disclosures attribute success to hard work or skill, but the FTC finds no basis given that these qualities distinguish successful from unsuccessful participants, and none acknowledges that saturation or lack of demand can constrain earnings regardless of effort.

claims.text: Network marketing success is a learnable skill rather than luck
claims.note: The UK Amway judgment quoted by Taylor found the thin top of the income 'candlestick' was those who had been IBOs longest (since 1979), while recent joiners and many long-term IBOs formed the base; position in the chain, not skill, drives outcomes.

claims.text: There is no shortcut in network marketing; it takes years of skill-building
claims.note: True that it is not quick; the omission is that years of effort still leave most participants with a loss.

claims.text: Dropshipping margins are thinner than buying inventory in bulk because the supplier takes a cut
claims.note: Per-unit supplier prices exceed bulk wholesale, and industry surveys put dropship margins well below private label.

claims.text: Dropshipping store owners depend on the supplier for stock, shipping speed and product quality
claims.note: The merchant never handles the goods, so stock-outs, delays and defects originate with the supplier.

claims.text: A dropshipping store owner stays responsible for customer service and returns even though the supplier ships
claims.note: Consumer law and marketplace rules hold the merchant of record responsible for the sale regardless of who ships.

claims.text: The hard part of dropshipping is products, suppliers and customer acquisition cost, not building the storefront
claims.note: Storefront tools are commoditized; product selection and customer acquisition cost are where most stores fail.

claims.text: Anyone can earn a large annual income by just earning a modest amount every day
claims.note: Dividing a target by days is arithmetic, not a method; median earnings show most people cannot sustain such a daily figure.

claims.text: Followers can be bought, so follower counts do not prove success
claims.note: Follower purchasing services are widely available and engagement ratios expose inflated counts.

claims.text: The first hundred thousand is the hardest; compounding makes later growth faster
claims.note: Compounding makes later increments larger, though the specific threshold is arbitrary.

claims.text: Higher income alone does not make people wealthy because spending rises to match
claims.note: Lifestyle inflation is well documented; surveys show many high earners living paycheck to paycheck.

claims.text: Paying off high-interest debt beats any investment return
claims.note: Paying down a debt at twenty-plus percent is a guaranteed return no diversified investment reliably matches.

claims.text: A one percent annual fee compounds into a large share of a portfolio over decades
claims.note: Fee drag compounds; standard calculators show one percent costing roughly a quarter of terminal wealth over thirty-plus years.

claims.text: Most actively managed funds underperform index funds after fees
claims.note: SPIVA scorecards consistently show most active funds trailing their benchmarks over ten-plus years.

claims.text: A first wholesaling fee takes months of daily cold calling to land
claims.note: Practitioner accounts agree first deals take months of outreach; many never close one.

claims.text: Distressed vacant properties yield the most motivated sellers
claims.note: Distress signals motivation, but no independent data compares lead-list conversion rates.

claims.text: Pricing offers off recently sold comparable properties avoids needing to estimate repair costs
claims.note: Comps help, but investors price on repair cost, so ignoring it leads to offers buyers reject.

claims.text: Short-term stock moves are unpredictable, so day trading is gambling
claims.note: Authors conclude that for prospective day traders trading to learn is no more rational or profitable than playing roulette, yet under 3% of traders are predictably profitable, so it is not pure chance.

claims.text: Gurus mix genuinely sound advice into pitches so the whole sales message seems trustworthy
claims.note: Describes a rhetorical tactic rather than a testable outcome.

claims.text: Trading jargon is used to manufacture an illusion of expertise that only the course can teach
claims.note: A claim about persuasion technique, not a measurable result.

claims.text: Day trading profits are taxed more heavily than long-term investing
claims.note: Short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income in the US, above long-term rates.

claims.text: Scaling one small product win across many products turns into thousands per month
claims.note: Most products fail to sell and each needs its own promotion, so one small win does not multiply into thousands a month.

claims.text: Micro-influencers get higher engagement and conversion than large accounts
claims.note: Engagement rates do fall as follower counts rise, but the conversion advantage rests mostly on marketing-vendor data.

claims.text: A .store domain gets more traffic and ranks higher on Google
claims.note: Search engines state the top-level domain does not affect ranking; the figure is a registry marketing claim.

claims.text: A paid course cannot remove the work or guarantee a dropshipping store will be profitable
claims.note: No course changes the product, supplier and acquisition economics that decide profitability.

claims.text: Only a small minority of course buyers ever complete the course
claims.note: Online course completion rates are commonly reported in the 5 to 15 percent range, though paid cohorts do better.

claims.text: Most people who try to sell their expertise as a course find little paying demand
claims.note: Course marketplaces show a long tail where most courses sell few or no copies.

claims.text: Course funnels never disqualify unfit buyers because the model depends on selling to them
claims.note: Funnels rarely screen buyers, but whether the business model requires unfit buyers is not established.

claims.text: Information is a small share of business success; execution is most of it
claims.note: A framing about what drives success, not a measurable split.

claims.text: A course that got results would not need massive ad spend, affiliates and hype seminars to sell
claims.note: An inference about marketing spend, not directly testable.

claims.text: Airbnb arbitrage requires the landlord's written consent and compliance with local short-term rental rules
claims.note: Subletting without consent breaches most leases, and many cities license or ban short-term rentals.

claims.text: Arbitrage profit is the spread between rent and booking revenue, so paying higher rent directly reduces it
claims.note: Booking revenue is set by the market, so rent is a direct subtraction from margin.

claims.text: Longer leases improve arbitrage returns by spreading furniture costs over more revenue
claims.note: Furniture is a fixed setup cost amortized over the lease term.

claims.text: Starting a short-term rental business in a downturn means cheap furniture and less competition
claims.note: Supply exits can lower competition and furniture costs, but downturns also cut travel demand and nightly rates.

claims.text: Anyone disciplined can build a six- or seven-figure Airbnb arbitrage business
claims.note: Market saturation, regulation and landlord refusals mean most entrants do not reach those revenues.

claims.text: Faceless YouTube automation channels run by freelancers can earn thousands per month on a couple hours of daily work
claims.note: Most automation channels never reach monetization and freelancer costs eat margins, so thousands a month on two hours a day is rare.

claims.text: Longer videos aimed at older US audiences earn higher YouTube ad revenue per view
claims.note: RPM varies by advertiser demand; US and older demographics and mid-roll ads on longer videos pay more.

claims.text: Click-through rate and retention decide whether YouTube promotes a video
claims.note: YouTube's recommendation system weights click-through and watch time, per its own documentation.

claims.text: Anyone who stays consistent will reach a thousand dollars a day from YouTube automation
claims.note: Consistency does not guarantee views; most channels never earn meaningful ad revenue.

claims.text: Rental property needs a large down payment plus cash reserves for repairs and vacancies
claims.note: Lenders require 15 to 25 percent down on investment property, and repairs and vacancies are routine costs.

claims.text: Crypto lending platforms pay high interest but are uninsured and can lose your deposit
claims.note: Several crypto lenders froze or lost customer deposits in 2022 bankruptcies.

claims.text: A thousand paying fans at ten dollars a month replaces a salary
claims.note: The arithmetic roughly holds after fees, but very few creators ever reach a thousand recurring paying fans.

claims.text: Millionaires have around seven income streams
claims.note: The seven-streams figure is repeated widely but no primary source confirms it.

claims.text: Beginner day traders fail because they chase large moves on small size instead of small frequent gains at scale
claims.note: Position sizing matters, but both approaches lose for most retail traders.

claims.text: A disciplined, proven strategy lets a retail day trader become consistently profitable
claims.note: Only 3.0% of persistent day traders were net profitable, 1.1% beat minimum wage and 0.5% a bank teller's wage, with no evidence of improvement with experience.

claims.text: Prove a strategy on small size before adding capital
claims.note: Practice advice.

claims.text: Investing a modest monthly sum for decades reaches a million through compounding
claims.note: Standard compound-growth arithmetic at historical equity returns.

claims.text: Nobody has lost money holding an S&P 500 index fund for twenty years or more
claims.note: True for every rolling twenty-year period in nominal terms since 1926, though real returns were near zero in a few.

claims.text: Starting to invest young matters most because time drives compounding
claims.note: Compounding scales with years invested.

claims.text: Organic TikTok and Instagram content can sell dropshipped products with no ad spend
claims.note: Organic virality does produce sales for some stores, but reach is unpredictable and most organic posts sell little.

claims.text: Viral views do not convert to sales when the audience is the wrong demographic
claims.note: Views from regions or audiences unlikely to buy do not convert, as ad-targeting data shows.

claims.text: Once the skills are mastered, online money falls out of thin air
claims.note: Even the source's own test needed daily filming for a week and yielded modest profit.

claims.text: Short organic dropshipping tests typically yield hundreds, not thousands, in profit
claims.note: Published first-hand tests typically report modest profits, but the sample is self-selected.

claims.text: Reposting old viral videos keeps sales going with no new work
claims.note: Platforms de-rank duplicate content and product interest fades, so reposting does not keep sales going without new work.

claims.text: Options have wider spreads and higher trading costs than stocks
claims.note: Average quoted bid-ask spread of S&P 500 stock options is 17.2% versus 3.55 bps for the stocks; retail's preferred sub-week options carry a 12.3% spread and PFOF for options is about double that for stocks.

claims.text: Even with a known edge, most people size bets so badly that many go bust
claims.note: The Haghani and Dewey biased-coin experiment found a large share of educated participants went bust.

claims.text: The best investors in history average around twenty percent a year, so retail traders should expect less
claims.note: Top long-run track records cluster near twenty percent annualized; retail averages are far below.

claims.text: Sports betting with bankroll management, small units and few parlays is consistently profitable
claims.note: Bankroll rules limit variance but do not create an edge; sportsbooks and pick'em apps price in a house margin.

claims.text: Betting only a few percent of bankroll per slip keeps a bettor in the game
claims.note: Small stakes reduce ruin risk but cannot overcome negative expected value.

claims.text: Betting platforms promote high-payout parlays because they are more profitable for the house
claims.note: Multi-leg parlays carry far higher hold percentages for operators.

claims.text: A bettor who keeps playing eventually loses winnings back to the house
claims.note: With a house edge, continued play converges to a loss by the law of large numbers.

claims.text: Each bet is independent, so a losing streak does not make a win due
claims.note: Independent events; the gambler's fallacy is well documented.

claims.text: Chasing losses emotionally is exactly what betting platforms profit from
claims.note: Loss-chasing is the core driver of gambling harm in behavioral research.

claims.text: Paid pick sellers force plays when losing to keep subscribers
claims.note: Plausible incentive but no systematic evidence on tipster behavior.

claims.text: Most of the very wealthy dropped out of college rather than graduating
claims.note: Surveys of the ultra-wealthy show a large majority hold degrees, many from elite schools.

claims.text: People with more education earn more on average
claims.note: CPS data 1970-2013, adjusted for worker characteristics: bachelor's graduates earned 56 percent and associate's graduates 21 percent more than high school graduates on average, and the premium at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles is nearly identical to the mean.

claims.text: Course sellers back claims with anecdotes rather than statistics
claims.note: DK Automation backed its profit claims with testimonials that did not reflect the experience of any consumer in the FTC's investigation, with disclaimers in unreadably small type; one documented instance.

claims.text: Market-rate investing alone will not make an ordinary saver rich within a decade
claims.note: At real after-tax returns near five percent, modest savings take decades to reach seven figures.

claims.text: After tax and inflation, market returns are roughly half the headline figure
claims.note: Taxes and roughly three percent inflation cut a ten percent nominal return to about half in real after-tax terms.

claims.text: Bubble-era returns on hyped assets are temporary and fade over the long term
claims.note: Bubble-era asset returns reverted after the dot-com and crypto cycles.

claims.text: Asset allocation drives returns more than picking individual securities
claims.note: Brinson-style attribution studies find allocation explains most return variation across portfolios.

claims.text: Most millionaires got there through business ownership, high income or saving, not a single investment
claims.note: Wealth surveys show business ownership, high earnings, saving and inheritance dominate millionaire origins.

claims.text: Options magnify both gains and losses relative to the underlying stock
claims.note: Options have leverage built into their price via delta and gamma.

claims.text: Beginners following paid or community trade signals typically lose money
claims.note: First-hand tests and brokerage data lean to losses, but signal quality varies and samples are small.

claims.text: Dropshipping on Amazon or eBay from retail marketplaces violates their terms and gets accounts banned
claims.note: eBay, Amazon US and Walmart rules quoted in the study prohibit buying from another retailer or marketplace and having it shipped to the customer, but the study also finds platforms suspend sellers only after enough reports, so such sellers often persist rather than being reliably banned.

claims.text: A dropshipping business still needs a seller's permit, sales tax collection and business registration
claims.note: Sales-tax nexus and licensing rules apply to any online merchant.

claims.text: Dropshipping is infinitely scalable because the work is the same at any volume
claims.note: Ad spend, customer service, refunds and supplier problems all grow with volume, so the work is not the same at any scale.

claims.text: Dropshipping is a stepping stone to private-label products, not a long-term model
claims.note: Strategic advice rather than a testable claim.

claims.text: Retail AI trading bots do not beat the market
claims.note: No retail trading bot has an audited record of beating the market; many are outright scams.

claims.text: Digital products become highly scalable once one finds a winner
claims.note: As a conditional this is true because digital goods have near-zero marginal cost; the claim stays silent on how rarely a winner is found.

claims.text: Most meme pages never make money
claims.note: Audience monetization is highly skewed; the vast majority of pages earn nothing.

claims.text: AI is a tool, not the business; money comes from solving problems people already pay for
claims.note: Framing about where value comes from.

claims.text: Using low-down-payment owner-occupant loans to buy many rentals is mortgage fraud that lenders detect
claims.note: Occupancy misrepresentation on a mortgage application is federal fraud and underwriters check recent loans.

claims.text: Low-down-payment conventional loans require living in the home for at least a year
claims.note: Conventional and FHA low-down loans require owner occupancy for at least twelve months.

claims.text: Authorized-user piggybacking raises a credit score fast but mortgage lenders discount it
claims.note: Scoring models and manual underwriting discount authorized-user tradelines.

claims.text: Good credit saves tens of thousands over the life of a mortgage
claims.note: One point of rate on a thirty-year loan compounds to tens of thousands in interest.

claims.text: Credit card limits rise automatically even when the card is barely used
claims.note: Issuers raise limits based on usage and payment history, and cut dormant lines.

claims.text: Buying flips on credit lines with minimal down payments fails on lender down-payment and debt-to-income rules
claims.note: Hard-money lenders require larger equity and lenders cap debt-to-income.

claims.text: Disputing credit-report items legally forces removal of anything not verified in time
claims.note: The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires removal of items not verified within thirty days.

claims.text: Get-rich-easy real estate pitches work by omitting the lending standards that make them impossible
claims.note: Describes a marketing omission, not a measurable outcome.

claims.text: Small business owners work more hours than their employees
claims.note: Incorporated self-employed work about 340 more hours a year than comparable full-time, full-year salaried workers and the unincorporated about 285 more after controls (raw CPS: 2,347 annual hours for incorporated vs 1,981 for salaried); the comparison is with salaried workers generally rather than owners' own employees.

claims.text: Most YouTube uploads never reach a thousand views, so luck dominates creator income
claims.note: A random sample of 10,016 YouTube videos found 86.93% had fewer than a thousand views and 65.44% fewer than a hundred, confirming the first half; the paper does not measure creator income or test whether luck explains it.

claims.text: Bank risk systems can miss unauthorized trades for months
claims.note: Repeated rogue-trader cases at major banks show controls catching unauthorized positions late.

claims.text: Trading mandates restrict which instruments a trader may trade, not just position size
claims.note: Standard bank mandate structure; instrument restrictions are part of every desk's limits.

claims.text: Bank trader bonuses are deferred and can be clawed back after losses or misconduct
claims.note: Deferred bonus and clawback rules have been standard at large banks since the 2008 reforms.

claims.text: Low-margin arbitrage desks tempt traders into hidden outsized risks
claims.note: An anecdotal pattern across a few rogue-trader cases, not an established finding.

claims.text: Most crypto assets are short-lived trends that must be sold before they collapse rather than held long term
claims.note: Most altcoins and memecoins have lost the large majority of their value from peak; only a handful have held value across cycles.

claims.text: Most altcoins never reclaim their prior-cycle highs when measured in Bitcoin
claims.note: True of most large altcoins across the 2017 and 2021 cycles, with a few exceptions.

claims.text: Traders who never withdraw gains watch paper fortunes evaporate
claims.note: Unrealized crypto gains routinely reverse by most of their value across cycles.

claims.text: A skilled trader can run meme coins or leveraged perps up to millions and then compound them
claims.note: Studies of leveraged retail crypto traders find the large majority lose money, so running small stakes to millions is a lottery outcome.

claims.text: Keeping most crypto holdings in a few established coins limits downside
claims.note: Bitcoin and Ethereum have drawn down 75-85% in bear markets, so the limit is relative.

claims.text: Casino games like roulette, craps, and slots carry a built-in house edge, so no betting system beats them long term
claims.note: House edge on these games is fixed by the rules; only card counting and skill games have known positive-EV play.

claims.text: Profitable sports betting comes from exploiting pricing discrepancies between sportsbooks, not sports knowledge
claims.note: Documented long-run edges are mostly price-based such as line shopping and beating the closing line, though some sharp bettors win with their own models.

claims.text: Sign-up bonus bets can be reliably turned into cash by betting both sides of an outcome
claims.note: Matched betting on promos is a well-documented small, one-time profit source.

claims.text: Arbitrage betting is not risk-free because a voided bet or human error can turn a small locked profit into a large loss
claims.note: Voided legs and palpable-error rules are standard sportsbook terms and are a known arb risk.

claims.text: Sportsbooks limit or ban bettors who show a consistent edge
claims.note: Limiting of winning accounts is widely reported and acknowledged by the books themselves.

claims.text: Sportsbooks push expert picks and analysis because they distract bettors from pricing, the only real edge
claims.note: A plausible incentive, but the motive is inferred rather than demonstrated.

claims.text: The vig on even-money bets takes a sizeable cut of every wager and has been rising
claims.note: Standard vig is around 4-5% on -110 lines; some markets are juiced higher, but the extreme figure is not typical.

claims.text: Subscription software can flag mispriced lines and reduce advantage betting to minutes a day
claims.note: Positive-EV tools do flag soft lines quickly, but sportsbooks limit winning accounts fast, so the edge is short-lived.

claims.text: Gambling addiction is a strong predictor of financial ruin
claims.note: Problem gambling is associated with bankruptcy, debt, and suicide in the public health literature.

claims.text: Debt is good if the asset it buys produces income that covers the payment with surplus, and bad if it funds consumption
claims.note: A definitional framing rather than a testable claim.

claims.text: Leverage magnifies losses as much as gains, so debt taken at the wrong time can set you back years
claims.note: Leveraged real estate investors were wiped out in 2008; the symmetry of leverage is arithmetic.

claims.text: Refinancing to return investors' capital leaves an infinite return with none of your own money in the deal
claims.note: A cash-out refinance can return capital only when values and rents cooperate, and the 'infinite return' framing ignores the larger loan, thinner cash flow and added risk.

claims.text: Credit card minimum payments cost more in interest than the original balance
claims.note: Standard amortization at 20% APR with minimum payments produces this result.

claims.text: Investors fund people with a track record, so you can control assets without your own capital
claims.note: Outside investors do back proven operators, but the typical reader has no track record and building one usually takes their own capital first.

claims.text: A sustained win rate above the sportsbook's implied probability yields profit over many bets despite individual losses
claims.note: As a conditional statement this is basic expected-value arithmetic; the hard part, which the claim does not deny, is having and keeping such an edge.

claims.text: Player prop markets are priced less sharply than main markets and offer more exploitable edges
claims.note: Props and other low-volume markets are widely documented as less efficient than main lines, though books offset this with low limits and quick restrictions.

claims.text: Betting as income requires a bankroll of thousands of dollars; small bankrolls only produce trivial profit
claims.note: Bankroll scales any real edge, but the premise that the edge exists is unproven.

claims.text: A self-reported bet tracker showing a high win rate proves a betting strategy works
claims.note: Unaudited trackers can omit bets, and a few months of results are dominated by variance.

claims.text: Parlays and exotic bets carry much larger house edges than straight bets
claims.note: Parlay hold percentages reported by books are several times those on straight bets.

claims.text: Trading gurus commonly present simulated or demo account results as real trading profits
claims.note: Regulators require simulated-results disclaimers because the practice is common; prevalence is not measured.

claims.text: Unregulated offshore brokers promoted by gurus can take deposits with no recourse
claims.note: Regulator warning lists and enforcement actions document offshore forex broker fraud.

claims.text: Influencers are paid to promote trading and crypto schemes to their audiences without clear disclosure
claims.note: Paid promotion of trading and crypto products by influencers is well documented and has drawn regulator action.

claims.text: Prop firms and brokers often delay or deny withdrawals to winning traders
claims.note: Widely reported in complaints; prevalence is unmeasured.

claims.text: Options spreads let small accounts take positions that would otherwise require far more capital
claims.note: Defined-risk spreads do reduce capital requirements; that is their mechanical purpose.

claims.text: Selling same-day iron condors collects premium with a defined maximum loss
claims.note: Mechanically correct; the maximum loss exceeds the premium and occurs on large moves.

claims.text: A deep in-the-money LEAPS call can earn more than owning the stock for less cash and less risk
claims.note: A deep in-the-money call needs less cash, but it adds leverage, time decay and the risk of losing the whole premium, so it is not less risky.

claims.text: Options strategies can grow a small account by double-digit percentages in a day
claims.note: A one-day double-digit gain needs positions that lose as much on adverse days, and most retail options traders lose money.

claims.text: Professional traders use options to cut capital and risk per trade
claims.note: Professionals do use options for capital efficiency and defined risk, but usually hedged and with risk controls retail traders lack.

claims.text: Doubling bets after each loss fails because bankrolls are finite and tables cap bet sizes
claims.note: Martingale ruin under a finite bankroll and bet limits is a textbook result.

claims.text: Long losing streaks are statistically inevitable over enough hands
claims.note: Follows directly from independent near-even bets.

claims.text: Ignoring a small house edge like the zero does not make a bet even
claims.note: The zero pockets are the entire source of the roulette house edge.

claims.text: Course sellers do not track or publish what fraction of their students make money
claims.note: Course sellers' own disclaimers state they do not track customer results.

claims.text: Agency middleman models add little value over hiring the freelancer directly
claims.note: Some agencies add strategy and accountability, but a reseller with no delivery skill competes against direct freelancer platforms.

claims.text: Students who succeed with guru programs usually had prior experience, connections, and savings
claims.note: Consistent with success-story patterns, but based on anecdotal reviews.

claims.text: Pyramid schemes pay mainly for recruiting new distributors rather than retail sales to outside customers
claims.note: In every one of the 350 MLM compensation plans Taylor analysed, rewards were paid primarily for aggressively recruiting a large downline rather than for retailing products to outside customers.

claims.text: Required inventory purchases, training fees, and marketing materials drain MLM participants beyond the low startup cost
claims.note: Beyond sign-up, Taylor found $50-$500 a month in incentivised product purchases needed to qualify for commissions, plus training, conferences, books, recordings and sales 'tools' that upline promoters expect downline participants to buy.

claims.text: Niche stores solving a specific problem for an underserved audience can succeed where generic stores fail
claims.note: Niche positioning is the pattern in surviving stores, but most niche stores still fail.

claims.text: Dropshipping can make an ordinary beginner a millionaire
claims.note: A few sellers reach that scale; the typical outcome is a loss, so the implied generality fails.

claims.text: AI makes starting an online business easier than ever
claims.note: AI tools do lower the cost and skill needed to start a store; the claim is about starting, though competing has become harder for the same reason.

claims.text: Only a tiny fraction of day traders earn persistent profits after costs, partly explained by chance
claims.note: Predictably profitable day traders are under 3% of all day traders on an average day and generate under 10% of day-trading volume.

claims.text: Day traders do not improve with experience; the longer they trade, the less likely they are profitable
claims.note: Share of profitable day traders falls monotonically with days traded (29.8% to 3.0%) and fixed-effects panel regressions on persistent traders find no learning; expected profit stays negative.

claims.text: Individual traders' losses are institutions' gains, because institutions provide liquidity to urgent uninformed orders
claims.note: Retail options trades lost $1.14bn while $4.13bn of effective-spread costs became revenue for market makers and exchanges executing retail orders; the liquidity-provision mechanism is asserted rather than tested.

claims.text: As all traders become more skilled, relative edges shrink and luck dominates outcomes
claims.note: The paradox-of-skill argument is well supported in sports and fund management; direct trading evidence is indirect.

claims.text: Individual investors buy attention-grabbing stocks, which then underperform
claims.note: Attention-driven buying and subsequent underperformance is a replicated finding.

claims.text: Paying for day trading education worsens prospects because there is no evidence traders learn
claims.note: Contrary to what brokerage specialists and course providers claim, there is no learning by day trading; expected profit is always negative and does not improve, though the effect of paid education itself is not tested.

claims.text: Many day traders trade for entertainment or the thrill of gambling rather than expected profit
claims.note: Authors argue persistent losers must be overconfident or derive non-financial utility (entertainment, gambling, impressing others) but cannot test the motives explicitly.

claims.text: Flippers reach full funding by stacking a first-position hard money loan with second-position private money
claims.note: Gap funding behind hard money is a standard flipper capital structure.

claims.text: Hard money lenders require a down payment plus points, fees, and double-digit interest
claims.note: Typical hard money terms are 10-20% down, 2-4 points, and 10-14% interest.

claims.text: Borrowing extra private money to cover the primary loan's fees lets a flipper enter a deal with no cash
claims.note: Stacking private money on a hard-money loan can cover entry costs, but it piles expensive debt on a thin spread where delays or overruns wipe out the profit.

claims.text: Any deal bought cheaply enough relative to after-repair value will find a lender
claims.note: Hard-money lenders readily fund deals at a deep discount to after-repair value, but borrower experience, credit and the lending cycle still decide, so 'any' overreaches.

claims.text: Giving up most of the profit to lenders is worth it to keep doing deals
claims.note: A preference about trade-offs, not a testable claim.

claims.text: Needlessly complex payout structures are a sign a scheme is hiding where returns come from
claims.note: A reasonable heuristic rather than a tested rule.

claims.text: Crypto schemes reach young audiences through gaming and streaming influencers
claims.note: Influencer-promoted tokens targeting young audiences are a documented pattern.

claims.text: Affiliate referral programs do not make ordinary participants rich
claims.note: Affiliate income distributions are heavily skewed; typical participants earn little.

claims.text: Advertised staking yields far above market rates are paid from new deposits or token inflation, not real revenue
claims.note: High fixed yields in 2021-22 schemes were funded by emissions and collapsed; some protocols do earn fees.

claims.text: Very few investors sustain returns far above the market for decades
claims.note: Persistence studies find almost no managers or individuals sustain large alpha.

claims.text: Investors boasting high returns usually have short track records that do not predict long-term results
claims.note: Short-window returns are dominated by variance and regime; persistence is rare.

claims.text: Leverage and options strategies that worked in a long bull market fail in a prolonged downturn
claims.note: Leveraged strategies suffer in drawdowns, though some hedged option strategies hold up.

claims.text: Free seminars exist to upsell attendees into far more expensive seminars
claims.note: The FTC alleges Nudge's free 90-minute seminars were predominantly a pitch for a $1,100+ three-day workshop, which in turn consisted largely of general information and a pitch for 'advanced training' costing up to $40,000.

claims.text: Few businesses reach the scale where the owner can step away and collect passive income
claims.note: Most small businesses are owner-operated with few or no employees.

claims.text: The real money in MLM comes from selling books, tapes, and seminar tickets to recruits
claims.note: Tools-and-training income for top distributors is documented in lawsuits, but its share of total MLM income is not measured.

claims.text: Generic get-rich advice cannot fit individual situations, so sweeping promises sell better than useful advice
claims.note: A framing about incentives, not a measurable claim.

claims.text: Published average day-trader salaries ignore the failure rate and overstate what a typical entrant earns
claims.note: Salary aggregators sample employed or surviving traders only.

claims.text: Most intraday trading profit is made in the first two hours after the market opens
claims.note: Volume and volatility peak at the open, but this is one trader's self-reported result.

claims.text: Faceless YouTube automation still demands constant hands-on management and is not passive
claims.note: Channel operators consistently report scripting, hiring, and managing editors as ongoing work.

claims.text: Viral hits from trends cannot be replicated and do not build a returning audience
claims.note: Trend-driven views churn; retention and returning viewers drive sustained channel revenue.

claims.text: Unreliable freelancers who vanish with project assets are a major cost of outsourced content
claims.note: A common complaint in outsourced creative work; frequency unmeasured.

claims.text: Gurus inflate how much faceless channels earn in order to sell their programs
claims.note: Consistent with earnings-claim patterns regulators have challenged; not measured for this niche.

claims.text: Faceless channels earn more from affiliate links and products than from AdSense
claims.note: Creator income surveys show sponsorships and products outweigh AdSense for most channels, but this needs an audience first.

claims.text: Paying someone to teach you is faster than learning by trial and error
claims.note: In a randomized trial of 432 Mexican small firms, a year of subsidized paid consulting raised productivity and return on assets by about a fifth of a standard deviation and employment by 44% years later, but did not raise sales or profits within the first year: paid expert help beat going it alone for existing firms, not for beginners buying online courses.

claims.text: Trading-education programs promising consistent market-beating profits are deceptive
claims.note: Day trading for a living is shown to be virtually impossible, contrary to what brokerage specialists and course providers often claim; the finding falsifies the promise without establishing intent to deceive.

claims.text: Sellers of money-making systems must have solid proof before making earnings claims
claims.note: The FTC Business Opportunity Rule bars earnings claims unless the seller has a reasonable basis, written substantiation, and gives prospects an earnings claim statement with the number and percentage of purchasers who achieved that level; a US legal requirement.

claims.text: Income-scheme promoters target people under financial stress
claims.note: Complaint data show spikes in income-scam reports during downturns.

claims.text: Choosing a business model with high gross margins matters more than the industry
claims.note: Margins matter, but execution and demand dominate outcomes.

claims.text: Chat-based sales and copywriting can earn six figures without calls or funnels
claims.note: Six-figure closers are the top tail of commission sales, and most people who try remote sales earn far less.

claims.text: Delegating low-value tasks frees an owner to focus on the work that grows the business
claims.note: Delegation is necessary to scale, but it is a management principle, not a guarantee of growth.

claims.text: Marketplaces provide built-in traffic but a suspended listing or algorithm change can erase revenue overnight
claims.note: Platform-dependency risk is widely documented among marketplace sellers.

claims.text: Digital products avoid suppliers and shipping and carry near-total margins
claims.note: Marginal cost is near zero; the cost shifts to creation and marketing.

claims.text: A brand-new standalone store gets no visitors until the owner drives traffic
claims.note: A standalone domain has no organic discovery; traffic must be bought or earned.

claims.text: Airbnb arbitrage pays fixed rent, so its downside is unbounded while co-hosting only shares revenue
claims.note: A fixed lease obligation against variable revenue is the structural risk of the model.

claims.text: Arbitrage units usually peak in their first year or two and then decline while rent keeps rising
claims.note: Consistent with rising short-term rental supply after 2022; based on one operator's portfolio.

claims.text: New competing short-term rental supply can turn a profitable unit cash-flow negative
claims.note: Revenue per listing fell in many US markets as supply grew after 2022.

claims.text: An arbitrage business cannot be sold; the only exit is dumping the furniture
claims.note: Lease-based operations have no transferable asset beyond furniture and lease assignment.

claims.text: Co-hosting for a percentage fee earns a similar margin to arbitrage with far less risk
claims.note: Management fees of 20-30% are standard; arbitrage upside is higher in good markets, downside unbounded.

claims.text: Early-2020s Airbnb arbitrage profits came from low rent and scarce supply that no longer exist
claims.note: Supply growth and rent increases since 2022 are documented, though some markets still work.

claims.text: Daily-upload finance influencers must invent new rules because the real advice fits on a postcard
claims.note: A framing about content incentives.

claims.text: Dropping out to build your own path works for a few with rare skills and luck, not for most people
claims.note: Earnings data show degree holders earn more on average; outliers exist.

claims.text: Earning a dollar self-employed is much harder than as an employee, and breaking even can take years
claims.note: Most new businesses take years to match a prior salary; many never do.

claims.text: Self-employment needs a multi-year savings runway before it covers living costs
claims.note: Runway advice is sensible; the right length varies by business.

claims.text: Self-employment is isolating and demands self-directed time management
claims.note: Surveys of the self-employed consistently report isolation and self-discipline as top challenges.

claims.text: The self-employed must set aside a large share of income for taxes and buy their own health insurance
claims.note: Self-employment tax covers both halves of payroll tax and no employer subsidizes insurance.

claims.text: A solo owner does every job, and constant task-switching is a mental cost
claims.note: Task-switching costs are documented in cognitive research; the business effect is anecdotal.

claims.text: Done-for-you Amazon automation packages costing tens of thousands rarely return the investment
claims.note: FTC alleges Empire/Automators sold automated-store packages at $10,000-$125,000 plus $15,000-$80,000 working capital, virtually no purchasers earned the advertised income, most lost their entire investment and nearly all stores were suspended; DK Automation's packages (up to $100,000) likewise left few consumers making money.

claims.text: The difficulty of finding profitable deals is the barrier that protects sellers who master it
claims.note: Skill barriers exist, but Amazon margins compress as competitors and fees rise.

claims.text: Overseas-to-doorstep dropshipping depended on a duty exemption for small packages and subsidized shipping that no longer exist
claims.note: De minimis was suspended in 2025 and subsidized postal rates ended; landed costs rose sharply.

claims.text: Shipping from a domestic warehouse cuts delivery to days and improves reviews at the cost of margin
claims.note: Domestic fulfillment delivers in days; the trade-off is higher unit cost.

claims.text: Private-labeling a validated product under your own brand raises margins and cuts returns
claims.note: Brand owners do report higher margins; the example is one seller's anecdote.

claims.text: Gurus adopt obnoxious personas because controversy earns free reach and fills the sales funnel
claims.note: Plausible funnel economics; the motive is inferred.

claims.text: Outrageous pitches filter the audience down to the most impressionable buyers, like scam emails with typos
claims.note: The typo-filter hypothesis for scam email has research support; the extension to gurus is inference.

claims.text: Selling skill takes years of practice, not a five-day seminar
claims.note: Sales performance develops over years of practice; no short course has demonstrated otherwise.

claims.text: Commission-based sales can out-earn most salaried jobs
claims.note: Top commissioned salespeople out-earn most employees, but median sales pay is ordinary and the 'can' only holds for the high performers.

claims.text: Investors who outsource decisions to advisors and chase FOMO get talked into get-rich-quick schemes
claims.note: Financial literacy correlates with avoiding fraud in surveys; the matrix itself is unvalidated.

claims.text: Financial freedom comes from financial literacy, tracking net worth, and a strategy rather than employment status
claims.note: A framework rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: Experts with access and trust can earn outsized returns by allocating other people's money
claims.note: Managers of other people's money can earn large fees and some deal access exists, but net returns from private deals are not reliably superior and the group is tiny.

claims.text: Money printing transfers wealth from savers and wage earners to debtors
claims.note: Unexpected inflation does favor fixed-rate borrowers, but real wages and asset returns vary; 'get rich' overstates it.

claims.text: Entrepreneurs and real estate investors can legally pay zero tax while high earners pay most of theirs
claims.note: Depreciation and exchanges can defer real-estate tax, but paying zero tax is an edge case, not the norm for entrepreneurs.

claims.text: The self-employed pay the highest taxes of all
claims.note: Self-employment tax adds both halves of payroll tax, but deductions offset it; it is not clearly the highest.

claims.text: Mindset determines outcomes; people afraid of losing their jobs generally lose them
claims.note: Teenage self-esteem and an internal locus of control (believing one controls one's future rather than fate or luck) predict later becoming an incorporated entrepreneur, alongside aptitude, family income and managerial aspirations; the paper does not test whether fear of job loss leads to job loss.

claims.text: Legal online sports betting reduces household savings and investment, especially in financially constrained households
claims.note: Staggered DiD on 230k households across 26 state legalizations: net brokerage deposits fall 14% overall and about 41% for low-savings households, with 2SLS implying $1 of betting cuts investment by $0.99 on average and $3.07 for low-savings households; effects grow over time and hold under alternative estimators (working paper, not peer-reviewed).

claims.text: Sports betting access also increases lottery play among households that already overdraw
claims.note: Legalization raises lottery spending, with households that recently overdrew increasing lotto play by about 9% of a standard deviation, while online poker is unaffected; caveat that the data capture only a small subset of lottery purchases.

claims.text: The true odds of sports bets are opaque, unlike lotteries and slots, so bettors cannot judge their expected loss
claims.note: Sports outcomes have no formulaic probability; the vig hides the expected loss.

claims.text: Phone-based betting enables impulsive wagering at any hour
claims.note: Mobile access drives most volume; the impulsivity link is argued rather than measured here.

claims.text: A new channel's first videos get almost no views until the algorithm learns who to show them to
claims.note: Recommendation systems need watch data before surfacing a new channel.

claims.text: Specific problem-solving titles get far more clicks than generic ones
claims.note: Click-through differences for specific versus generic titles are widely reported by creators.

claims.text: Multiple faceless channels can generate five figures a month
claims.note: Most faceless channels never reach monetization, and five-figure monthly claims come from operators selling courses.

claims.text: Paid mentorship gives a guru visibility into students' winning products, which can be copied to compete against them
claims.note: A documented allegation in this case; prevalence across mentorships is unknown.

claims.text: Spending the course fee on test ads teaches more than any course
claims.note: Across 580 comparisons, explicit instruction produced better learning than unassisted discovery (d = 0.38), and the authors conclude unassisted discovery does not benefit learners while feedback and worked examples do: trial and error alone is the weaker teacher, though the studies are classroom and lab tasks, not ad testing.

claims.text: Even profitable day traders rarely earn a living wage from it
claims.note: Of 47 net-profitable persistent day traders, only 17 earned above Brazilian minimum wage (US$16/day) and 8 above a bank teller's starting pay (US$54/day), the latter with daily standard deviations of US$632-3,308.

claims.text: Only a small minority of third-party Amazon sellers earn even a modest income
claims.note: Seller surveys show many sellers make little, but the share depends on how dormant and part-time accounts are counted.

claims.text: Trading on borrowed money can leave traders in debt beyond their original stake
claims.note: The FCA warns that margin close-out is not a guaranteed stop-loss, so in volatile markets leveraged CFD clients could lose their entire deposit or sustain losses exceeding it, leaving them owing money to the firm.

claims.text: Celebrity endorsements are not evidence that a speculative asset is a sound investment
claims.note: Celebrity-promoted tokens have repeatedly collapsed and regulators have fined undisclosed paid promotions.

claims.text: Most retail crypto buyers who entered during a boom lost money in the following crash
claims.note: Across 95 countries 73% of crypto-exchange app users first downloaded when Bitcoin was above $20,000 (its Oct 2022 price), and a $100-a-month simulation from first download puts 75-81% of users underwater with a median loss of 48%; returns are simulated from entry timing, not observed account P&L.

claims.text: Most retail options trades lose money, with losses far larger than on stock trades
claims.note: Retail (wholesaler-executed) options trades lost $1.14bn in aggregate over Nov 2019-Jun 2021 at a 10-day horizon, before $4.13bn of spread costs, concentrated in sub-week at-the-money calls; measured in aggregate, not per trade, and not compared with stock trades.

claims.text: Retail investors trade options for lottery-like payoffs and entertainment rather than hedging
claims.note: Retail options trades are 69% calls, mostly at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money, half in sub-week expiries, patterns the authors read as speculation rather than hedging.

claims.text: Retail traders bid up option prices before earnings announcements and lose when volatility subsides
claims.note: de Silva, Smith and So document retail losses of five to fourteen percent around earnings announcements from overpaying for implied volatility.

claims.text: Brokerages promote options trading because payment for order flow makes it highly profitable for them
claims.note: Wholesalers pay brokerages for order flow, giving brokers an incentive to encourage more trading in wider-spread assets; in Q2 2021 PFOF was $581m for options versus $284m for stocks, and options are prominent on gamified apps.

claims.text: Seeing other traders' wins makes people take more risk and trade more
claims.note: An experimental study found this effect and social-trading platform data point the same way, though effect sizes vary.

claims.text: Complex multi-leg options strategies lose more for retail traders than simple ones
claims.note: One 2023 study finds this; the result is recent and not yet widely replicated.

claims.text: Retail option-trading losses accrue mainly to market makers and wholesalers
claims.note: Indirect costs of $4.13bn paid by retail option traders through effective spreads become revenue for market makers and exchanges, five times direct commissions and three times the raw trading loss.

claims.text: Hustle-culture sellers typically started with family money, income or a supportive spouse rather than hustle
claims.note: Plausible and anecdotally common, but no systematic survey of guru backgrounds exists.

claims.text: Successful side hustles rest on a marketable skill, not on hours worked
claims.note: Survey data show professional-services side hustles earn the most, supporting the skill mechanism, though effort still matters.

claims.text: Retail traders hold losing option positions open after announcements even though volatility has subsided
claims.note: The study documents a disposition-effect pattern consistent with the broader retail-investor behaviour literature.

claims.text: Retail options trading has grown many-fold since commission-free trading apps appeared
claims.note: Dollar volume of retail-origin (SLAN) and small option trades grew 143% and 224% between Nov 2019 and Jul 2021; strong growth but the data start in 2019 so growth since 2015 is not measured.

claims.text: Retail traders are drawn to options on firms with heavy media coverage
claims.note: Retail share in options is higher on smaller, higher-volume underlyings and correlates with WallStreetBets mentions and Robinhood ownership, consistent with attention-grabbing names; media coverage per se is not measured.

claims.text: High market valuations predict lower future returns but too weakly to time the market profitably
claims.note: AQR's out-of-sample tests show valuation-based timing adds little or negative value after 1958.

claims.text: Missing a handful of the best trading days sharply cuts long-run returns
claims.note: Arithmetically true for every major index, though missing the worst days would help as much; neither is predictable.

claims.text: Lump-sum investing beats dollar-cost averaging most of the time
claims.note: Vanguard's 2012 study and later replications find lump sum wins about two-thirds of twelve-month periods.

claims.text: No investor has timed the market successfully and consistently
claims.note: Mutual-fund and newsletter studies find no persistent timing skill, though it is a strong universal claim.

claims.text: Predicting short-term stock market moves is not a learnable expertise because markets lack regular feedback
claims.note: Kahneman and Klein's conditions for expertise and forecaster track-record studies support this.

claims.text: Selling stocks because they look expensive bets against momentum
claims.note: Momentum is one of the most robust return anomalies and valuation signals fire while prices are still rising.

claims.text: Motivational hustle content lifts mood but is not practical advice
claims.note: Framing about how to interpret a genre of content.

claims.text: Copying already-viral product videos onto an under-served platform reliably produces sales
claims.note: Reposting proven content raises the odds somewhat, but virality is largely luck and competitors copy the same videos, so it does not reliably produce sales.

claims.text: Dropshipping without paid ads yields high profit margins because marketing is the largest cost
claims.note: Ad spend is usually the largest cost, but organic traffic is unreliable and fees, refunds, chargebacks and labor still cut margins well below the gross figure.

claims.text: Brand-deal and ad-share creator income stops as soon as posting stops
claims.note: Platform ad revenue tracks views and brand deals are per-campaign; back-catalogue income exists but is small for most.

claims.text: Creators who earn a living mostly own a recurring-revenue product rather than relying on brand deals
claims.note: Creator surveys show brand deals remain the largest income source for most full-time creators, and the claim comes from a vendor.

claims.text: Most creator income comes from brand deals, the most volatile revenue source
claims.note: Goldman Sachs estimates about seventy percent from brand deals; the volatility claim is reasonable but not measured.

claims.text: Word-of-mouth testimonials are the most powerful form of advertising
claims.note: Recommendations from people you know are the most trusted ad source in surveys, but in MLMs they mostly reach friends and family and exhaust quickly.

claims.text: MLM distributors earn recurring commissions whenever a referred customer reorders
claims.note: Compensation plans do pay on customer reorders, but income disclosures show most distributors have few retail customers and earn little or nothing.

claims.text: Recruiting a downline gives MLM participants leverage and scalable income
claims.note: Downline-based commissions and rank bonuses exist, but the rank tables show over 90% of participants in the lowest cohort averaging under $100 while six-figure incomes belong to hundredths of a percent; the leverage is real only for a tiny fraction.

claims.text: MLMs provide built-in training and support that ordinary entrepreneurs lack
claims.note: Training exists but is an expense: the FTC lists training materials, conferences and trainings among participant costs, and comments describe paid weekly meetings, $100 conference tickets and required audio subscriptions.

claims.text: Duplicating a simple sales system across a team lets an MLM business scale like franchises
claims.note: Unlike franchises, recruits have no territory or customer base and the chain must grow geometrically to pay the levels above.

claims.text: Backtesting a strategy on past charts overstates how it performs live
claims.note: Look-ahead bias, overfitting and the absence of execution costs and emotion make backtests systematically optimistic.

claims.text: Day trading for a month teaches useful skills even if it does not make money
claims.note: Whether the skills are worth the time is a matter of judgement.

claims.text: Nobody gets rich from a month of day trading
claims.note: Even the best documented traders compound slowly; month-level outcomes for beginners are dominated by noise and losses.

claims.text: Network marketing, direct sales and peer-to-peer marketing are the same recruitment pyramid under different names
claims.note: The terms are used interchangeably by MLMs, though some direct-sales models pay no recruitment-based commissions.

claims.text: Paying for recruits' event tickets is used to create guilt and reinforce company doctrine
claims.note: Consistent with ex-member accounts and high-control-group literature but not systematically measured.

claims.text: Retail investors often fail to exercise options optimally, adding to their losses
claims.note: Higher retail trading in a contract strongly predicts the fraction of in-the-money calls left suboptimally unexercised on cum-dividend dates, and the effect grows for the most profitable-to-exercise contracts, pointing to investor mistakes.

claims.text: Investors accept low expected returns on lottery-like assets because of the small chance of a huge payoff
claims.note: The skewness or lottery preference is a robust asset-pricing finding across stocks, options and other assets.

claims.text: Copying the habits of successful people does not work because the unsuccessful share the same habits
claims.note: Selecting on the outcome makes habit correlations uninformative; base-rate failure data for founders and creators bears this out.

claims.text: Airbnb arbitrage can be started with no money and no property by managing landlords' units for a commission
claims.note: Co-hosting for a commission needs little capital, but landlords rarely hand units to strangers without a track record.

claims.text: Every city's short-term-rental regulations contain loopholes that allow the business
claims.note: Many cities restrict short-term rentals to primary residences or ban them outright, which rules out arbitrage entirely.

claims.text: Furnished rentals that sit unlet for weeks signal landlords who will accept a short-term-rental deal
claims.note: A stale listing shows vacancy cost, but willingness also hinges on lease terms, building rules and liability.

claims.text: A property earns roughly double as a short-term rental what it earns as a long-term rental
claims.note: Gross short-term revenue can beat rent in strong markets, but net of fees, cleaning, vacancy and management the premium is far smaller and often negative.

claims.text: Revenue-estimate reports from analyzer tools reliably predict what a listing will earn
claims.note: Analyzer tools extrapolate from established listings and tend to overstate earnings for new hosts.

claims.text: The typical side hustle earns a few hundred dollars a month, far below the headline average
claims.note: Survey data consistently show heavily right-skewed side-hustle earnings with a low median.

claims.text: Most side-hustle income goes to living expenses or discretionary spending rather than building wealth
claims.note: Bankrate finds only a minority save any of it; consistent with other surveys.

claims.text: Side hustling rises when the job market weakens and prices rise
claims.note: Plausible and consistent with the survey trend, but it is an analyst's interpretation rather than a tested relationship.

claims.text: A typical side hustle can pay off an average credit-card balance within months
claims.note: The figure uses mean side-hustle income; at the median it would take years, not months.

claims.text: Younger adults are more likely than older ones to have a side hustle
claims.note: Consistent across several independent side-hustle surveys.

claims.text: A large share of side hustlers expect to always need one to make ends meet
claims.note: Survey finding; a self-reported expectation.

claims.text: Trading firms rarely disclose what share of their clients lose money
claims.note: EU CFD brokers must publish client loss percentages, typically seventy to eighty percent; US stock and options brokers have no such requirement.

claims.text: Rising shipping, goods and advertising costs are squeezing Amazon seller margins
claims.note: Vendor survey of self-selected sellers; consistent with Amazon fee increases and ad-cost inflation.

claims.text: Established brands see third-party Amazon sellers as a serious competitive threat
claims.note: Survey sentiment; third-party sellers do account for over half of Amazon unit sales.

claims.text: Amazon sellers are shifting sourcing away from China toward domestic suppliers
claims.note: Vendor survey; tariff pressure makes it plausible but the base of US sourcing is small.

claims.text: Advertising on Amazon has become a required and growing expense for sellers
claims.note: Amazon's advertising revenue has grown faster than its marketplace and organic placement has shrunk.

claims.text: Get-rich-quick pitches work by exploiting fear of failure and desire for status
claims.note: Consistent with consumer-protection research on business-opportunity fraud and loss-aversion marketing.

claims.text: Long hours pay off only when spent on work one is passionate about
claims.note: Motivational framing; passion is neither necessary nor sufficient for income.

claims.text: Guru business models depend on customers failing and buying more
claims.note: Upsell funnels are documented, but customers who succeed become testimonials, so the incentive is mixed.

claims.text: Reinvesting early side-hustle profits into tools, marketing and outsourcing is what lifts a side hustle into the top tier
claims.note: Reinvesting is needed to grow, but it cannot fix a business with no demand, and crediting top earners' success to it is survivorship bias.

claims.text: Sizing up only after a daily profit cushion and adding to winners makes day-trading results consistent
claims.note: Position sizing can reshape the daily P&L pattern but cannot create an edge; the consistency evidence is one trader's own record.

claims.text: TikTok Shop affiliate videos can earn beginners a full-time income from product commissions
claims.note: Affiliate commission income is heavily skewed: a few creators earn large sums while most affiliates earn little or nothing.

claims.text: Financing purchases through your own whole life policy recaptures the interest you used to pay banks
claims.note: The recaptured payments are your own savings plus loan interest paid to the insurer; the gain comes from paying off debt or saving, which works without a policy.

claims.text: Borrowing against a whole life policy lets the full cash value keep compounding while you use the money
claims.note: Policy loans leave cash value in place earning credits, but the loan accrues interest and some insurers cut dividends on borrowed sums, so the net gain is only the spread.

claims.text: Borrowing from your policy at a lower rate than its dividend rate earns a spread that grows every year
claims.note: The dividend rate is not the policy's net return after insurance costs; long-run cash-value returns are a few percent and loan rates are often similar, so the spread is small or negative.

claims.text: A mature infinite-banking policy returns far more than each year's premium, beating any bank or fund
claims.note: This counts growth on all prior premiums as a return on one year's deposit; measured properly, whole life cash value compounds at low single digits.

claims.text: Whole life cash value is a tax-free, liquid, guaranteed savings vehicle
claims.note: Growth is tax-deferred and loans untaxed if the policy stays in force and avoids MEC status, but only a low base rate is guaranteed, dividends are not, and early surrender loses money.

claims.text: Standard whole life policies pay agents most of the first-year base premium as commission, leaving little early cash value
claims.note: First-year whole life commissions commonly run from half to all of the base premium, and early cash values sit far below premiums paid.

claims.text: Directing premiums into paid-up additions riders gives a whole life policy much higher early cash value
claims.note: Paid-up-addition riders carry low commissions and add cash value quickly, which is why high-cash-value designs use them within IRS MEC limits.

claims.text: Mass cold messaging on social media reliably recruits MLM distributors if you do enough of it
claims.note: Volume outreach yields a trickle of sign-ups at very low conversion, but it is spam that platforms restrict and the recruits rarely earn money.

claims.text: Spotting under-the-radar small-cap altcoins early lets retail buyers capture ten-fold or greater gains
claims.note: Most small-cap tokens lose most of their value or die; promoter-picked gems are a lottery where a few big winners hide many losers.

claims.text: Altcoins rally once Bitcoin confirms an uptrend because confidence and risk appetite rotate into them
claims.note: Altcoins are highly correlated with Bitcoin and have sometimes rallied after it, but broad alt seasons are irregular and many altcoins keep losing ground to Bitcoin.

claims.text: Beginners can earn a steady weekly income from forex within months using a simple strategy
claims.note: Regulator-mandated broker disclosures show most retail forex and CFD accounts lose money, and few beginners become consistently profitable.

claims.text: Forex trading is the most profitable business to start because it has no customers, products or operations
claims.note: Most retail forex accounts lose money per brokers' own disclosures, so as a business it is worse than most, not the best.

claims.text: Setting a profit target larger than the stop-loss gives a trader an edge by itself
claims.note: Wider targets are hit less often, so the risk-reward ratio alone does not change expected value; an edge needs entries with predictive power.

claims.text: A stop-loss guarantees a trade cannot lose more than the planned amount
claims.note: Stops cap losses in normal conditions, but gaps, slippage and fast markets can fill well beyond the stop.

claims.text: Trading only in the direction of the prevailing trend raises the odds of a winning trade
claims.note: Trend-following has modest documented returns in currencies over months, but reading the trend off a chart gives little short-term edge after costs.

claims.text: UGC creators are paid for the content itself, so they can earn without any following
claims.note: UGC deals pay for content and usage rights on brand channels, so follower count matters far less than in influencer deals.

claims.text: A beginner UGC creator can reach a few thousand dollars a month within three months
claims.note: UGC is crowded with new creators and many land few or no paid deals; the stated ramp is the seller's own figures, not measured outcomes.

claims.text: Personalized cold pitches and repeated follow-ups are how new freelancers land their first clients
claims.note: Personalized outreach and follow-up raise reply rates, but response rates stay low and many first deals come from referrals and platforms.

claims.text: Third-party tracking of a signal provider's account makes its performance claims trustworthy
claims.note: Verified tracking confirms trades on one account but cannot rule out cherry-picked or demo accounts, and past results do not predict future ones.

claims.text: Beginners can buy investment real estate with no money of their own
claims.note: Lenders require down payments on investment property; no-money deals depend on partners, sellers or a track record most beginners lack.

claims.text: Real estate is forgiving enough that even a mistaken purchase still makes money
claims.note: Leveraged property bought badly can and often does lose money, as foreclosure waves show; early wins in rising markets do not generalize.

claims.text: Family and friends are the cheapest source of money for a first real estate deal
claims.note: Family loans can cost less than hard money, but they are not free, and a failed deal puts relationships at risk as well as money.

claims.text: Buying an established TikTok account is a safe shortcut past creator follower requirements
claims.note: TikTok's terms bar buying and selling accounts, bought accounts risk bans, and she herself warns many sellers are scams.

claims.text: A self-publishing business scales to six figures by publishing more and better books
claims.note: Self-published book income is extremely skewed and most titles sell few copies, so volume alone does not reliably reach six figures.

claims.text: A book topic is profitable if competing books on it already sell well on Amazon
claims.note: Existing sales show demand, but a new low-review book competes with established titles and most self-published books sell few copies.

claims.text: Sales and recruiting are a numbers game: contacting enough people makes up for a lack of skill
claims.note: More contacts do mechanically yield more yeses, but conversion rates and saturated personal networks cap it, and in MLMs more recruits rarely means profit.

claims.text: Prospects usually need several exposures before joining or buying, so persistent follow-up drives recruiting and sales
claims.note: Multi-touch follow-up is standard sales practice, but the specific exposure count is folklore and persistence does not make an MLM opportunity profitable.

claims.text: A beginner can make a steady hundred dollars a day buying options on a small account
claims.note: Most retail options buyers lose money, and a steady daily income from a few thousand dollars implies returns far beyond any documented sustained performance.

claims.text: Buying call options just before earnings is a proven way to double money quickly
