claims.note: Implied volatility is bid up before earnings and collapses after the announcement, so pre-earnings option buyers lose on average.

claims.text: In-the-money options with delta above one half have better than even odds of ending in profit
claims.note: Delta roughly approximates the chance of expiring in the money, not of clearing the premium paid, so the probability of profit is lower than delta.

claims.text: Buying calls when a stock shows positive momentum or gaps up is an easy way to make money
claims.note: Short-term momentum and gap patterns offer at most weak edges that option premiums and spreads absorb; most retail option buyers lose.

claims.text: Whole life insurance cash value can be accessed through policy loans without the taxes and penalties of retirement accounts
claims.note: Policy loans are generally untaxed and penalty-free, but they accrue interest, early surrender charges apply, and a lapse with loans outstanding can trigger tax.

claims.text: Whole life cash value is part of the death benefit, so you cannot collect both
claims.note: In standard whole life the insurer pays the face amount minus outstanding loans; the cash value is not paid on top.

claims.text: A beginner can build an AI automation agency to a full-time income within a year
claims.note: Agency success stories are survivors; most new service businesses earn little in their first year and agency-course audiences crowd the same market.

claims.text: Workflow-automation skills can be learned from free videos in a couple of weeks well enough to sell to businesses
claims.note: No-code tools are quick to learn for simple workflows, but reliable client systems and selling them take longer for most beginners.

claims.text: Asking everyone you know for referrals reliably lands a new service business its first client
claims.note: Warm-network referrals are a common source of first clients, but results depend heavily on the network and are not reliable for everyone.

claims.text: Working for free for the first clients is the fastest way to start a service business
claims.note: Free work can buy testimonials and experience, but it also attracts low-commitment clients and does not reliably convert to paid work.

claims.text: Remote high-ticket closing for online coaching offers lets a beginner earn a large income quickly on commission
claims.note: Commission closers depend on an offer's lead flow and most quit within weeks; large quick earnings come from the few placed on top influencer offers.

claims.text: A commission closer's income depends more on the offer's lead flow than on sales skill
claims.note: Commission scales with qualified call volume, which the offer controls, though skill still sets the close rate.

claims.text: Joining a remote-sales community gets beginners placed on high-ticket closing offers regardless of experience
claims.note: Placement claims come from the communities that sell or promote them and have no independent data.

claims.text: Affiliate links layered into existing content add income that runs on autopilot
claims.note: Affiliate links earn small commissions passively once content has traffic, but without an audience they earn nothing.

claims.text: Running a paid online community or membership gives an ordinary creator recurring monthly income
claims.note: A few large communities earn well, but most paid communities have few members and high churn; the earnings shown are platform outliers.

claims.text: Buying a course with master resell rights lets a beginner earn immediately by reselling it and keeping all the profit
claims.note: Master-resell-rights schemes sell the same course to buyers who mostly earn by recruiting further buyers, so the market saturates; the FTC has acted against such income claims.

claims.text: UGC creators can land monthly retainers from brands for recurring videos
claims.note: Retainers exist for established creators, but brands increasingly pay per asset or on performance and beginners rarely get them.

claims.text: TikTok's algorithm can push a single video from a tiny account to millions of views
claims.note: TikTok distributes by interest rather than follower count, so small accounts occasionally go viral, though it is rare.

claims.text: Niche does not matter for short-form content because the creator's personality is the differentiator
claims.note: A framing about creative strategy with no clear evidence either way.

claims.text: Print-on-demand lets a beginner with no inventory build a business earning thousands a month
claims.note: Print-on-demand margins are thin and marketplaces saturated; most sellers make few sales, and the revenue examples shown are outliers.

claims.text: Recreating already-trending designs with AI is the easiest way to get print-on-demand sales
claims.note: Following proven demand helps, but copied trend designs face heavy competition and risk copyright and trademark takedowns.

claims.text: Print-on-demand margins are thin because the printer's base cost takes most of the sale price
claims.note: Base costs on major print-on-demand platforms leave a few dollars per item before fees, ads and refunds.

claims.text: Paid ads only amplify products that already sell; they cannot fix a weak product
claims.note: Ad performance follows product appeal and creative; ads on unproven listings mainly burn budget.

claims.text: A print-on-demand store can be started with no money because the printer is paid only after a sale
claims.note: Pop-up and marketplace integrations take payment before fulfilment so there is no upfront cost, though samples and traffic still cost money or time.

claims.text: Pinterest works as a free search-driven traffic source for print-on-demand stores
claims.note: Pinterest can send search traffic to product pins, but results for new accounts are slow and uncertain.

claims.text: Matched betting earns a few thousand dollars a month on one set of accounts after several months
claims.note: Matched betting is low-risk, but bonus supply is finite and accounts get restricted; typical sustained profits are a few hundred a month, not thousands.

claims.text: Matched betting gives a fixed mathematical edge, so profit keeps growing the longer you do it
claims.note: The promotional edge is real, but bookmakers restrict profitable accounts over time, so returns decline rather than keep growing.

claims.text: Scaling matched betting through other people's bookmaker accounts breaks terms and risks confiscated balances
claims.note: Bookmaker terms bar betting on accounts not your own, and operators void bets and withhold balances when they detect it.

claims.text: Copying the structure of already-converting product videos is the most reliable way to make affiliate content sell
claims.note: Imitating proven formats raises hit rates somewhat, but saturation and duplicate-content penalties limit the gain.

claims.text: Creator videos licensed as paid ads earn creators far more than organic affiliate commission
claims.note: Payout figures come from a brand owner recruiting creators; there is no independent data on typical earnings.

claims.text: Sales calls that amplify a prospect's pain and imagined future reliably close high-ticket coaching sales
claims.note: Problem-focused emotional selling does raise conversion, but closes still depend on qualified demand, and high-pressure tactics draw regulator scrutiny.

claims.text: Students can earn well freelancing or tutoring a skill they already have on flexible hours
claims.note: Tutoring and freelance work pay real hourly rates, but platform competition is heavy and income stays tied to hours.

claims.text: Raising prices attracts buyers who will pay almost any price to solve their problem, so most sellers should charge premium prices
claims.note: Some sellers underprice, but demand is price-sensitive for most offers; anecdotes of raised prices selling more are selected cases.

claims.text: Paying for high-ticket coaching returns many times its cost
claims.note: The returns cited are selected client testimonials; no independent data shows typical buyers recover high coaching fees.

claims.text: Sellers must buy premium offers themselves to be able to sell premium offers
claims.note: A motivational framing that also serves to sell the speaker's own premium coaching.

claims.text: A product's markup over its unit cost is a return comparable to or better than stock-market returns
claims.note: Markup ignores overhead, marketing and capital at risk; it is not an annual return on invested capital and cannot be compared to market returns.

claims.text: Unusual options-flow alerts reveal institutional orders that retail day traders can profitably follow
claims.note: Order flow carries some information in academic data, but public flow alerts arrive late and noisy, and nothing shows retail traders profit from following them.

claims.text: Short-dated, just-out-of-the-money options are the best day-trading instrument because they are cheap and react most to price moves
claims.note: Retail option losses are concentrated in short-dated out-of-the-money contracts, where time decay and spreads eat the leverage.

claims.text: An AI automation agency can be built to a million-dollar annual run rate within a month from a small budget
claims.note: New service agencies take months or years to sign clients; a month-one seven-figure run rate is far outside any base rate.

claims.text: Small businesses will pay thousands of dollars a month for custom AI chatbots and workflow automations
claims.note: Off-the-shelf chatbot and automation tools cost tens to hundreds a month, so few small businesses pay agency retainers in the thousands for them.

claims.text: Setting a very short deadline makes work get done faster because work expands to fill the time available
claims.note: Deadlines do curb procrastination, but planning-fallacy research shows tight deadlines are routinely missed and can cut quality.

claims.text: Paying prop-firm challenge fees is an investment because the first payouts recover the fees lost on blown accounts
claims.note: Most challenge buyers never get funded or paid, so for the typical buyer the fees are a sunk loss, not tuition that pays back.

claims.text: A cheap prop-firm challenge can be passed within days, giving a trader a large funded account
claims.note: Industry figures put challenge pass rates in the single digits to low teens, and funded accounts are usually simulated with tight drawdown rules.

claims.text: Trading a funded prop-firm account can replace a full-time income
claims.note: Firms that disclosed data show only a small share of funded traders ever receive a payout, and fewer receive repeated ones.

claims.text: Bracketing a major economic release with buy and sell stop orders can pass a prop-firm evaluation in a single trade
claims.note: News spikes cause slippage and whipsaw fills, many firms ban news trading, and the presenter herself calls it gambling.

claims.text: Prop-firm challenge fees are effectively risk-free because they are refunded after passing
claims.note: The refund comes only after passing and usually after a first payout, which most buyers never reach, so the fee is usually lost.

claims.text: Buying a property subject to the seller's existing mortgage lets an investor acquire it without a new loan or down payment
claims.note: Subject-to deals are legal and do happen, but the lender can call the loan under the due-on-sale clause and motivated sellers with assumable equity are scarce.

claims.text: Holding a rental for a few years while tenants pay the mortgage and then selling it yields a large lump-sum profit
claims.note: Sale profits depend mostly on local appreciation and selling costs; in flat or falling markets, like the 2009 crash she describes, there is no lump sum.

claims.text: Real-estate crowdfunding lets an ordinary investor raise other people's money to buy property with none of their own
claims.note: Raising a fund means securities-law filings, offering costs and a track record investors trust; first-timers rarely raise money this way.

claims.text: Trading apps that filter scam and bundled tokens make meme coin trading safe
claims.note: Filters catch some rug pulls, but most meme coins still collapse toward zero and most traders of them lose money.

claims.text: A rising US manufacturing index signals an upcoming altcoin season
claims.note: The link rests on a couple of past cycles; with so few data points it has no demonstrated predictive power for altcoin prices.

claims.text: Holding altcoins with conviction through drawdowns is how investors capture bull-market gains
claims.note: Most altcoins never regain prior highs, so holding through drawdowns usually locks in losses rather than gains.

claims.text: Crypto markets grow bigger each cycle as institutions and ETFs adopt them
claims.note: Total crypto market cap has made higher peaks across cycles and ETF access grew, but most individual tokens shrank, and past cycles do not guarantee the next.

claims.text: Staying out of the range between pre-market and prior-day highs and lows avoids most losing day trades
claims.note: No independent test of this filter exists; the support is the seller's own picked backtest days.

claims.text: Opening-range breakouts confirmed by a retest give retail day traders a reliable edge
claims.note: Published tests of opening-range breakout rules show small, unstable edges that mostly vanish after costs, and most retail day traders still lose.

claims.text: Institutions deliberately sweep retail stop-loss clusters at obvious levels, so trading the reversal after a sweep is a reliable edge
claims.note: Stops do cluster at round and recent levels, but no independent evidence shows retail traders profit from fading these sweeps.

claims.text: A stay-at-home parent can earn meaningful income selling digital printables on Etsy working only during nap times
claims.note: Most Etsy shops earn very little, and digital printables are flooded with resold templates, so one seller's results don't carry over to most parents.

claims.text: Listing products with high search volume and low competition, optimized for marketplace search, brings sales without ads or social media
claims.note: Marketplace search does drive organic sales, but keyword-tool competition scores are rough and the low-competition gaps fill quickly.

claims.text: Private-label-rights templates let sellers list new digital products quickly without creating them from scratch
claims.note: PLR templates do cut creation time, though the same templates go to many sellers, so the listings are hard to tell apart.

claims.text: Online marketplace sales peak in the fourth-quarter holiday season
claims.note: US retail and e-commerce sales follow a well-documented seasonal peak from October through December.

claims.text: Low-content books timed to holidays can earn hundreds of dollars a day even with poor reviews
claims.note: The figures are tool estimates for a handful of top sellers; most low-content books sell few or no copies in a crowded category.

claims.text: Publishing books for a different holiday each season keeps print-on-demand income steady through the year
claims.note: Stacking seasonal titles smooths income somewhat, but each holiday spike is short and competitive and the fourth quarter still dominates.

claims.text: Following the right crypto influencer lets an investor get rich without relying on luck
claims.note: Influencer coin picks show no persistent skill, and many promoted tokens underperform after the promotion.

claims.text: Audience engagement with a crypto video pushes up the prices of the coins it promotes
claims.note: Influencer attention can move tiny coins briefly, but it has no lasting effect on large caps like the ones listed, and the bumps tend to reverse.

claims.text: A partnership with a major asset manager makes a crypto token a good investment
claims.note: Partnerships rarely send value to a token's holders, and the news is usually priced in by the time it is announced.

commonlyWrong.text: Technical patterns such as Fibonacci retracements and fair value gaps predict where price will react
commonlyWrong.note: Academic tests of Fibonacci and similar chart levels find no predictive power beyond chance; the golden-ratio-in-nature justification is numerology.

commonlyWrong.text: Beginners with no experience can make real money with AI side hustles because the tools do the hard part.
commonlyWrong.note: In a randomized trial of 640 Kenyan small-business owners given a GPT-4 business mentor, the average effect on revenue and profit was not distinguishable from zero and only above-median performers gained (about 15%), while below-median performers did nearly 10% worse: the tool did not do the hard part for the weakest operators (existing businesses in Kenya over two months, not beginners starting AI side hustles).

commonlyWrong.text: Using bank debt to buy cash-flowing rental property is how ordinary people become rich
commonlyWrong.note: Leveraged rentals built some fortunes, but most ordinary households build wealth through home equity and retirement savings, and leverage magnifies losses.

commonlyWrong.text: A digital product built once earns passive income for years while you sleep
commonlyWrong.note: Most digital products sell almost nothing without continual promotion, so passive income for years is the rare case.

commonlyWrong.text: Funded-trader (prop firm) accounts let beginners trade size without their own capital
commonlyWrong.note: Most evaluation-based prop firm customers fail and pay repeated fees, and few beginners ever trade funded size or get paid.

commonlyWrong.text: An experienced day trader can multiply a small account many times over within a month by trading momentum stocks.
commonlyWrong.note: Among 1,551 persistent futures day traders the single best earned US$310 a day on average with a daily standard deviation of US$2,560, and only 0.5% beat a bank teller's wage; nobody shows multiplying an account in a month, though the setting is Brazilian index futures rather than momentum stocks.

commonlyWrong.text: Identifying crypto narratives early (AI agents, meme coins, new chains) is how investors capture outsized returns
commonlyWrong.note: The winning examples are survivorship-selected; most narrative and meme tokens lose most of their value and retail buyers rarely get in early.

commonlyWrong.text: Network marketing success is a learnable skill rather than luck
commonlyWrong.note: The UK Amway judgment quoted by Taylor found the thin top of the income 'candlestick' was those who had been IBOs longest (since 1979), while recent joiners and many long-term IBOs formed the base; position in the chain, not skill, drives outcomes.

commonlyWrong.text: Once a trader has a consistently profitable setup, profits scale by simply increasing position size
commonlyWrong.note: Liquidity, slippage and market impact erode edges as size grows, especially in thin small caps, so profits do not scale by simply sizing up.

commonlyWrong.text: TikTok Shop affiliate videos can earn beginners a full-time income from product commissions
commonlyWrong.note: Affiliate commission income is heavily skewed: a few creators earn large sums while most affiliates earn little or nothing.

commonlyWrong.text: Trading a funded prop-firm account can replace a full-time income
commonlyWrong.note: Firms that disclosed data show only a small share of funded traders ever receive a payout, and fewer receive repeated ones.

commonlyWrong.text: Uploading self-published books to Amazon produces ongoing royalties with little further work
commonlyWrong.note: The median self-published title earns almost nothing and the store is flooded with low-content books, so ongoing royalties with little work is not the typical result.

commonlyWrong.text: Buyers of paid ecommerce coaching are much more likely to succeed than people using free content
commonlyWrong.note: Success rates come from vendor testimonials, and regulators have found most buyers of such coaching do not recoup their fees.

commonlyWrong.text: AI can replace subject expertise when creating an information product.
commonlyWrong.note: Marketplaces are flooded with generic AI-written products, and buyers pay for trust and depth that expertise provides.

commonlyWrong.text: A cheap prop-firm challenge can be passed within days, giving a trader a large funded account
commonlyWrong.note: Industry figures put challenge pass rates in the single digits to low teens, and funded accounts are usually simulated with tight drawdown rules.

commonlyWrong.text: AI-drafted digital products decouple income from hours because they sell repeatedly at zero marginal cost.
commonlyWrong.note: Zero marginal cost is real, but most digital products sell very few copies and selling them takes ongoing hours of marketing.

commonlyWrong.text: Most ecommerce side-hustle failures come from poor execution, not from a broken business model
commonlyWrong.note: Rising ad costs, copycat competition and thin margins are structural and sink well-executed stores too.

commonlyWrong.text: Options strategies can grow a small account by double-digit percentages in a day
commonlyWrong.note: A one-day double-digit gain needs positions that lose as much on adverse days, and most retail options traders lose money.

commonlyWrong.text: Saving cash is a losing strategy because fiat money has lost value since leaving the gold standard
commonlyWrong.note: Inflation erodes idle cash, but an emergency fund and a high savings rate are among the strongest predictors of household wealth.

commonlyWrong.text: Anyone can reach several thousand dollars a month of passive cash flow within a year if they decide to
commonlyWrong.note: MLM income disclosures and small-business survival data show the large majority of people who try earn little or nothing in the first year.

commonlyWrong.text: Anyone who can talk to an AI can build and sell a software app without coding
commonlyWrong.note: AI builders make prototypes, but reliable sellable software and finding paying users remain out of reach for most non-coders.

commonlyWrong.text: Anyone who stays consistent will reach a thousand dollars a day from YouTube automation
commonlyWrong.note: Consistency does not guarantee views; most channels never earn meaningful ad revenue.

commonlyWrong.text: A beginner can sell small-business websites built with AI tools at prices comparable to freelance web designers.
commonlyWrong.note: Small businesses can build basic sites themselves with the same tools, and beginners without a portfolio struggle to charge designer rates.

commonlyWrong.text: A beginner UGC creator can reach a few thousand dollars a month within three months
commonlyWrong.note: UGC is crowded with new creators and many land few or no paid deals; the stated ramp is the seller's own figures, not measured outcomes.

commonlyWrong.text: Content creators whose content is good and algorithm-friendly will succeed; luck is no longer the main factor
commonlyWrong.note: Experiments on cultural markets show large randomness in outcomes at similar quality, and most channels never reach monetization.

commonlyWrong.text: Drop-servicing, a marketing front-end that subcontracts local service work, earns margin without doing or knowing the work
commonlyWrong.note: Lead arbitrage exists, but ad costs, licensing, liability and contractor quality make margin without knowing the work unreliable for most.

commonlyWrong.text: Dropshipping can make an ordinary beginner a millionaire
commonlyWrong.note: A few sellers reach that scale; the typical outcome is a loss, so the implied generality fails.

commonlyWrong.text: Dropshipping is infinitely scalable because the work is the same at any volume
commonlyWrong.note: Ad spend, customer service, refunds and supplier problems all grow with volume, so the work is not the same at any scale.

commonlyWrong.text: Financing purchases through your own whole life policy recaptures the interest you used to pay banks
commonlyWrong.note: The recaptured payments are your own savings plus loan interest paid to the insurer; the gain comes from paying off debt or saving, which works without a policy.

commonlyWrong.text: Going full-time on a side hustle multiplies its income far beyond the extra hours because commitment forces it to work
commonlyWrong.note: Survivor anecdotes aside, people who quit jobs for ventures often see income fall, and commitment does not create demand.

commonlyWrong.text: Investors fund people with a track record, so you can control assets without your own capital
commonlyWrong.note: Outside investors do back proven operators, but the typical reader has no track record and building one usually takes their own capital first.

commonlyWrong.text: Landlords will agree to short-term-rental subleasing if offered a rent bonus and professional cleaning
commonlyWrong.note: Most landlords refuse subleasing on lease, insurance and building-rule grounds, and a small bonus rarely changes that.

commonlyWrong.text: Launching enough digital products guarantees an eventual hit.
commonlyWrong.note: Repeated attempts raise the odds but guarantee nothing, and most sellers quit or run out of money before a hit.

commonlyWrong.text: Leverage lets a small account take large positions while keeping the dollar amount at risk fixed
commonlyWrong.note: ESMA: leverage raises the probability of a larger loss more than of a larger gain, automatic margin close-out reduces but does not eliminate the risk of losing all or more than the initial margin, and in gapping markets the investor may be unable to close at their preferred price, so the amount at risk is not fixed.

commonlyWrong.text: A mature infinite-banking policy returns far more than each year's premium, beating any bank or fund
commonlyWrong.note: This counts growth on all prior premiums as a return on one year's deposit; measured properly, whole life cash value compounds at low single digits.

commonlyWrong.text: Opening-range breakouts confirmed by a retest give retail day traders a reliable edge
commonlyWrong.note: Published tests of opening-range breakout rules show small, unstable edges that mostly vanish after costs, and most retail day traders still lose.

commonlyWrong.text: Print-on-demand lets a beginner with no inventory build a business earning thousands a month
commonlyWrong.note: Print-on-demand margins are thin and marketplaces saturated; most sellers make few sales, and the revenue examples shown are outliers.

commonlyWrong.text: Prop-firm challenge fees are effectively risk-free because they are refunded after passing
commonlyWrong.note: The refund comes only after passing and usually after a first payout, which most buyers never reach, so the fee is usually lost.

commonlyWrong.text: Refinancing to return investors' capital leaves an infinite return with none of your own money in the deal
commonlyWrong.note: A cash-out refinance can return capital only when values and rents cooperate, and the 'infinite return' framing ignores the larger loan, thinner cash flow and added risk.

commonlyWrong.text: Remote high-ticket closing for online coaching offers lets a beginner earn a large income quickly on commission
commonlyWrong.note: Commission closers depend on an offer's lead flow and most quit within weeks; large quick earnings come from the few placed on top influencer offers.

commonlyWrong.text: Revenue-estimate reports from analyzer tools reliably predict what a listing will earn
commonlyWrong.note: Analyzer tools extrapolate from established listings and tend to overstate earnings for new hosts.

commonlyWrong.text: A skilled trader can run meme coins or leveraged perps up to millions and then compound them
commonlyWrong.note: Studies of leveraged retail crypto traders find the large majority lose money, so running small stakes to millions is a lottery outcome.

commonlyWrong.text: If someone in your company reached the top, you can too regardless of background
commonlyWrong.note: 64 of 70 disclosures attribute success to hard work or skill, but the FTC finds no basis given that these qualities distinguish successful from unsuccessful participants, and none acknowledges that saturation or lack of demand can constrain earnings regardless of effort.

commonlyWrong.text: A trader who is net profitable over ten tracked practice trades is ready to trade real money
commonlyWrong.note: Ten trades is far too small a sample to distinguish an edge from luck; statistical tests of trading skill need hundreds of trades.

commonlyWrong.text: Wholesaling needs almost no money because earnest deposits are small, refundable and can be borrowed.
commonlyWrong.note: Deposits can be small, but finding discounted sellers takes paid data and marketing, and deposits are often at risk once contingencies lapse.

commonlyWrong.text: Word-search puzzle books sell well on KDP because few sellers can make them
commonlyWrong.note: Free puzzle generators are widely available and the category is saturated with near-identical listings, so the premise of few sellers is false.

commonlyWrong.text: Affiliate marketing needs no special skills or experience to earn a full-time income
commonlyWrong.note: Affiliate income depends on building an audience or search traffic, which is a skilled, slow process; most affiliates earn little.

commonlyWrong.text: Any side hustle can be scaled into a multi-million-dollar business
commonlyWrong.note: Most small businesses never grow past a handful of employees, so scaling any side hustle to millions is a rare exception.

commonlyWrong.text: Anyone can earn a large annual income by just earning a modest amount every day
commonlyWrong.note: Dividing a target by days is arithmetic, not a method; median earnings show most people cannot sustain such a daily figure.

commonlyWrong.text: Anyone disciplined can build a six- or seven-figure Airbnb arbitrage business
commonlyWrong.note: Market saturation, regulation and landlord refusals mean most entrants do not reach those revenues.

commonlyWrong.text: Audience engagement with a crypto video pushes up the prices of the coins it promotes
commonlyWrong.note: Influencer attention can move tiny coins briefly, but it has no lasting effect on large caps like the ones listed, and the bumps tend to reverse.

commonlyWrong.text: An AI automation agency can be built to a million-dollar annual run rate within a month from a small budget
commonlyWrong.note: New service agencies take months or years to sign clients; a month-one seven-figure run rate is far outside any base rate.

commonlyWrong.text: A beginner can build an AI automation agency to a full-time income within a year
commonlyWrong.note: Agency success stories are survivors; most new service businesses earn little in their first year and agency-course audiences crowd the same market.

commonlyWrong.text: A beginner can make a steady hundred dollars a day buying options on a small account
commonlyWrong.note: Most retail options buyers lose money, and a steady daily income from a few thousand dollars implies returns far beyond any documented sustained performance.

commonlyWrong.text: Beginners can buy investment real estate with no money of their own
commonlyWrong.note: Lenders require down payments on investment property; no-money deals depend on partners, sellers or a track record most beginners lack.

commonlyWrong.text: Beginners can earn a steady weekly income from forex within months using a simple strategy
commonlyWrong.note: Regulator-mandated broker disclosures show most retail forex and CFD accounts lose money, and few beginners become consistently profitable.

commonlyWrong.text: Bitcoin follows a four-year halving cycle with predictable peaks, year-long corrections and deep drawdowns
commonlyWrong.note: Three past cycles loosely fit the pattern, which is too few to call peaks predictable, and ETF-era flows have already broken the timing.

commonlyWrong.text: Borrowing from your policy at a lower rate than its dividend rate earns a spread that grows every year
commonlyWrong.note: The dividend rate is not the policy's net return after insurance costs; long-run cash-value returns are a few percent and loan rates are often similar, so the spread is small or negative.

commonlyWrong.text: Bracketing a major economic release with buy and sell stop orders can pass a prop-firm evaluation in a single trade
commonlyWrong.note: News spikes cause slippage and whipsaw fills, many firms ban news trading, and the presenter herself calls it gambling.

commonlyWrong.text: Buying call options just before earnings is a proven way to double money quickly
commonlyWrong.note: Implied volatility is bid up before earnings and collapses after the announcement, so pre-earnings option buyers lose on average.

commonlyWrong.text: Buying calls when a stock shows positive momentum or gaps up is an easy way to make money
commonlyWrong.note: Short-term momentum and gap patterns offer at most weak edges that option premiums and spreads absorb; most retail option buyers lose.

commonlyWrong.text: Buying a course with master resell rights lets a beginner earn immediately by reselling it and keeping all the profit
commonlyWrong.note: Master-resell-rights schemes sell the same course to buyers who mostly earn by recruiting further buyers, so the market saturates; the FTC has acted against such income claims.

commonlyWrong.text: Buying an established TikTok account is a safe shortcut past creator follower requirements
commonlyWrong.note: TikTok's terms bar buying and selling accounts, bought accounts risk bans, and she herself warns many sellers are scams.

commonlyWrong.text: Chat-based sales and copywriting can earn six figures without calls or funnels
commonlyWrong.note: Six-figure closers are the top tail of commission sales, and most people who try remote sales earn far less.

commonlyWrong.text: An AI chatbot can validate a product's market potential before spending on ads
commonlyWrong.note: A chatbot can summarize public signals but cannot measure conversion rates or ad costs, so it cannot validate whether a product will sell profitably.

commonlyWrong.text: Chinese sellers and tariffs are not a real threat to a well-branded consumable product
commonlyWrong.note: China-based sellers now hold a large share of Amazon marketplace listings and tariff changes have squeezed many FBA margins, so the threat is real even for branded consumables.

commonlyWrong.text: Committing fully with no plan B is the key to success in network marketing
commonlyWrong.note: Commitment does not change the structural payout; income disclosures show nearly all participants lose regardless of effort.

commonlyWrong.text: Copying already-viral product videos onto an under-served platform reliably produces sales
commonlyWrong.note: Reposting proven content raises the odds somewhat, but virality is largely luck and competitors copy the same videos, so it does not reliably produce sales.

commonlyWrong.text: Creators who earn a living mostly own a recurring-revenue product rather than relying on brand deals
commonlyWrong.note: Creator surveys show brand deals remain the largest income source for most full-time creators, and the claim comes from a vendor.

commonlyWrong.text: Day trading lets a small account earn in a single day what long-term investing earns in a year on the same risk
commonlyWrong.note: Persistent futures day traders had negative expected daily profit (mean -US$48.81, 97% losing) with large volatility, the opposite of earning a year's investment return in a day at equal risk.

commonlyWrong.text: A deep in-the-money LEAPS call can earn more than owning the stock for less cash and less risk
commonlyWrong.note: A deep in-the-money call needs less cash, but it adds leverage, time decay and the risk of losing the whole premium, so it is not less risky.

commonlyWrong.text: A digital product priced modestly needs only a few sales a week to become an easy income
commonlyWrong.note: The arithmetic works, but most self-published digital products sell close to nothing, so a few sales a week is not easy.

commonlyWrong.text: Duplicating a simple sales system across a team lets an MLM business scale like franchises
commonlyWrong.note: Unlike franchises, recruits have no territory or customer base and the chain must grow geometrically to pay the levels above.

commonlyWrong.text: Entrepreneurs and real estate investors can legally pay zero tax while high earners pay most of theirs
commonlyWrong.note: Depreciation and exchanges can defer real-estate tax, but paying zero tax is an edge case, not the norm for entrepreneurs.

commonlyWrong.text: Every city's short-term-rental regulations contain loopholes that allow the business
commonlyWrong.note: Many cities restrict short-term rentals to primary residences or ban them outright, which rules out arbitrage entirely.

commonlyWrong.text: Faceless YouTube automation channels run by freelancers can earn thousands per month on a couple hours of daily work
commonlyWrong.note: Most automation channels never reach monetization and freelancer costs eat margins, so thousands a month on two hours a day is rare.

commonlyWrong.text: Following the right crypto influencer lets an investor get rich without relying on luck
commonlyWrong.note: Influencer coin picks show no persistent skill, and many promoted tokens underperform after the promotion.

commonlyWrong.text: Forex trading is the most profitable business to start because it has no customers, products or operations
commonlyWrong.note: Most retail forex accounts lose money per brokers' own disclosures, so as a business it is worse than most, not the best.

commonlyWrong.text: Holding altcoins with conviction through drawdowns is how investors capture bull-market gains
commonlyWrong.note: Most altcoins never regain prior highs, so holding through drawdowns usually locks in losses rather than gains.

commonlyWrong.text: Institutions deliberately sweep retail stop-loss clusters at obvious levels, so trading the reversal after a sweep is a reliable edge
commonlyWrong.note: Stops do cluster at round and recent levels, but no independent evidence shows retail traders profit from fading these sweeps.

commonlyWrong.text: Low-content books timed to holidays can earn hundreds of dollars a day even with poor reviews
commonlyWrong.note: The figures are tool estimates for a handful of top sellers; most low-content books sell few or no copies in a crowded category.

commonlyWrong.text: Making money is a learnable skill, not luck; a skilled person could rebuild wealth from nothing within a decade
commonlyWrong.note: Skill raises the odds, but research on entrepreneurial and wealth outcomes finds a large luck component, so neither 'not luck' nor a reliable decade-long rebuild holds.

commonlyWrong.text: Matched betting earns a few thousand dollars a month on one set of accounts after several months
commonlyWrong.note: Matched betting is low-risk, but bonus supply is finite and accounts get restricted; typical sustained profits are a few hundred a month, not thousands.

commonlyWrong.text: In-the-money options with delta above one half have better than even odds of ending in profit
commonlyWrong.note: Delta roughly approximates the chance of expiring in the money, not of clearing the premium paid, so the probability of profit is lower than delta.

commonlyWrong.text: Multiple faceless channels can generate five figures a month
commonlyWrong.note: Most faceless channels never reach monetization, and five-figure monthly claims come from operators selling courses.

commonlyWrong.text: Once the skills are mastered, online money falls out of thin air
commonlyWrong.note: Even the source's own test needed daily filming for a week and yielded modest profit.

commonlyWrong.text: One arbitraged short-term rental unit nets a couple of thousand dollars a month once set up
commonlyWrong.note: Market data show falling revenue per listing and many arbitraged units earning below rent and costs, so a couple of thousand net is not typical.

commonlyWrong.text: Paid coaching gives a better return than a college degree
commonlyWrong.note: The college wage premium is large and well measured, while coaching returns rest on self-reported, selected testimonials.

commonlyWrong.text: Paid social ads are a learnable skill in days and a money machine for any product
commonlyWrong.note: Ad platforms are easy to use but hard to profit from, and many small advertisers never reach a positive return.

commonlyWrong.text: A partnership with a major asset manager makes a crypto token a good investment
commonlyWrong.note: Partnerships rarely send value to a token's holders, and the news is usually priced in by the time it is announced.

commonlyWrong.text: Paying for high-ticket coaching returns many times its cost
commonlyWrong.note: The returns cited are selected client testimonials; no independent data shows typical buyers recover high coaching fees.

commonlyWrong.text: Paying prop-firm challenge fees is an investment because the first payouts recover the fees lost on blown accounts
commonlyWrong.note: Most challenge buyers never get funded or paid, so for the typical buyer the fees are a sunk loss, not tuition that pays back.

commonlyWrong.text: With personal coaching a beginner can build a six-figure Amazon business within a year
commonlyWrong.note: Automators' $5,000 one-on-one Amazon coaching advertised students making $10,000+ a month, but the FTC alleges virtually none of its coaching clients made the advertised amounts and most did not recoup their investment.

commonlyWrong.text: Print-on-demand t-shirts on Amazon earn passive income if you find small untapped niches
commonlyWrong.note: Tier limits, saturation and takedowns keep typical print-on-demand royalties small, and untapped niches close fast once found.

commonlyWrong.text: A product's markup over its unit cost is a return comparable to or better than stock-market returns
commonlyWrong.note: Markup ignores overhead, marketing and capital at risk; it is not an annual return on invested capital and cannot be compared to market returns.

commonlyWrong.text: A property earns roughly double as a short-term rental what it earns as a long-term rental
commonlyWrong.note: Gross short-term revenue can beat rent in strong markets, but net of fees, cleaning, vacancy and management the premium is far smaller and often negative.

commonlyWrong.text: Proprietary buy/sell indicators reliably flag over- and undervalued zones to trade
commonlyWrong.note: Oscillator-style indicators are lagging transforms of price; no independent evidence shows paid indicator suites produce an edge after costs.

commonlyWrong.text: Public stock investing is a scam because the investor cannot control the outcome
commonlyWrong.note: Diversified index investing has delivered positive real returns over every long period on record; lack of control is not fraud.

commonlyWrong.text: Publishing a book or course makes you an authority that prospects say yes to before hearing the offer
commonlyWrong.note: Authority signals help conversion modestly, but most self-published books and courses reach few readers and do not presell prospects.

commonlyWrong.text: Raising prices attracts buyers who will pay almost any price to solve their problem, so most sellers should charge premium prices
commonlyWrong.note: Some sellers underprice, but demand is price-sensitive for most offers; anecdotes of raised prices selling more are selected cases.

commonlyWrong.text: Real-estate crowdfunding lets an ordinary investor raise other people's money to buy property with none of their own
commonlyWrong.note: Raising a fund means securities-law filings, offering costs and a track record investors trust; first-timers rarely raise money this way.

commonlyWrong.text: Real estate is forgiving enough that even a mistaken purchase still makes money
commonlyWrong.note: Leveraged property bought badly can and often does lose money, as foreclosure waves show; early wins in rising markets do not generalize.

commonlyWrong.text: Reposting old viral videos keeps sales going with no new work
commonlyWrong.note: Platforms de-rank duplicate content and product interest fades, so reposting does not keep sales going without new work.

commonlyWrong.text: Retail investors have a stronger edge in crypto than in stocks because they are not competing with institutions and insiders
commonlyWrong.note: On-chain data show small holders (<1 BTC) buy as Bitcoin rises while whales and miners sell, so larger and more sophisticated investors profit at retail's expense even in calm periods, and 73-81% of retail entrants likely lost money; retail is the counterparty of insiders, not free of them.

commonlyWrong.text: A rising US manufacturing index signals an upcoming altcoin season
commonlyWrong.note: The link rests on a couple of past cycles; with so few data points it has no demonstrated predictive power for altcoin prices.

commonlyWrong.text: Running a paid online community or membership gives an ordinary creator recurring monthly income
commonlyWrong.note: A few large communities earn well, but most paid communities have few members and high churn; the earnings shown are platform outliers.

commonlyWrong.text: A running short-term rental needs only about an hour a week of the operator's time
commonlyWrong.note: Guest messaging, turnover coordination, maintenance and reviews take far more unless a paid manager is hired, which cuts profit.

commonlyWrong.text: Scaling one small product win across many products turns into thousands per month
commonlyWrong.note: Most products fail to sell and each needs its own promotion, so one small win does not multiply into thousands a month.

commonlyWrong.text: Scraped directory websites can earn passive ad or lead income for near-zero cost; it is a numbers game across many sites
commonlyWrong.note: Search engines demote thin scraped and aggregator sites, so most such directories earn nothing and are not passive.

commonlyWrong.text: AI script writing removes the main barrier that stops beginners from starting a YouTube channel
commonlyWrong.note: Discoverability and retention, not scripts, are the binding constraints, and AI lowers the scripting barrier for every competitor equally.

commonlyWrong.text: A self-publishing business scales to six figures by publishing more and better books
commonlyWrong.note: Self-published book income is extremely skewed and most titles sell few copies, so volume alone does not reliably reach six figures.

commonlyWrong.text: A self-reported bet tracker showing a high win rate proves a betting strategy works
commonlyWrong.note: Unaudited trackers can omit bets, and a few months of results are dominated by variance.

commonlyWrong.text: Setting a profit target larger than the stop-loss gives a trader an edge by itself
commonlyWrong.note: Wider targets are hit less often, so the risk-reward ratio alone does not change expected value; an edge needs entries with predictive power.

commonlyWrong.text: Short-dated, just-out-of-the-money options are the best day-trading instrument because they are cheap and react most to price moves
commonlyWrong.note: Retail option losses are concentrated in short-dated out-of-the-money contracts, where time decay and spreads eat the leverage.

commonlyWrong.text: Short-term rental arbitrage scales linearly by adding units
commonlyWrong.note: Each unit needs fresh capital, a willing landlord and more management, and regulation caps many markets, so linear scaling is a best case.

commonlyWrong.text: Sizing up only after a daily profit cushion and adding to winners makes day-trading results consistent
commonlyWrong.note: Position sizing can reshape the daily P&L pattern but cannot create an edge; the consistency evidence is one trader's own record.

commonlyWrong.text: Small businesses will pay thousands of dollars a month for custom AI chatbots and workflow automations
commonlyWrong.note: Off-the-shelf chatbot and automation tools cost tens to hundreds a month, so few small businesses pay agency retainers in the thousands for them.

commonlyWrong.text: Small RV or mobile-home parks bought with seller financing are many times more profitable than single-family rentals
commonlyWrong.note: Park yields run somewhat higher than single-family rentals for more work and risk, not many times higher, and low-cash seller financing is rare.

commonlyWrong.text: Spending the course fee on test ads teaches more than any course
commonlyWrong.note: Across 580 comparisons, explicit instruction produced better learning than unassisted discovery (d = 0.38), and the authors conclude unassisted discovery does not benefit learners while feedback and worked examples do: trial and error alone is the weaker teacher, though the studies are classroom and lab tasks, not ad testing.

commonlyWrong.text: Sports betting with bankroll management, small units and few parlays is consistently profitable
commonlyWrong.note: Bankroll rules limit variance but do not create an edge; sportsbooks and pick'em apps price in a house margin.

commonlyWrong.text: Spotting under-the-radar small-cap altcoins early lets retail buyers capture ten-fold or greater gains
commonlyWrong.note: Most small-cap tokens lose most of their value or die; promoter-picked gems are a lottery where a few big winners hide many losers.

commonlyWrong.text: Starting a business with no money is a competitive advantage because well-funded founders lose imagination and discipline
commonlyWrong.note: Family income is a powerful predictor of becoming an incorporated entrepreneur: a $100,000 higher 1979 family income is associated with an almost 60% higher probability of incorporation after controlling for ability, traits and education, which the authors read as credit constraints materially hindering entrepreneurship; the paper tests entry rather than founder discipline, but points the opposite way to the claim.

commonlyWrong.text: Starting or joining a startup is the most reliable way to get rich by compressing a career's work into a few years.
commonlyWrong.note: Startups produce many self-made fortunes, but most fail and median founder and early-employee payoffs are near zero, so they are high-variance rather than reliable.

commonlyWrong.text: A stay-at-home parent can earn meaningful income selling digital printables on Etsy working only during nap times
commonlyWrong.note: Most Etsy shops earn very little, and digital printables are flooded with resold templates, so one seller's results don't carry over to most parents.

commonlyWrong.text: A stop-loss guarantees a trade cannot lose more than the planned amount
commonlyWrong.note: Stops cap losses in normal conditions, but gaps, slippage and fast markets can fill well beyond the stop.

commonlyWrong.text: A .store domain gets more traffic and ranks higher on Google
commonlyWrong.note: Search engines state the top-level domain does not affect ranking; the figure is a registry marketing claim.

commonlyWrong.text: Students of dropshipping coaching programs collectively generate tens of millions in sales
commonlyWrong.note: Empire consistently claimed hundreds of clients generating over $150 million in revenue; the FTC alleges this was false and most clients lost money, so this type of aggregate-sales claim was fabricated in at least this case.

commonlyWrong.text: Trading apps that filter scam and bundled tokens make meme coin trading safe
commonlyWrong.note: Filters catch some rug pulls, but most meme coins still collapse toward zero and most traders of them lose money.

commonlyWrong.text: A typical side hustle can pay off an average credit-card balance within months
commonlyWrong.note: The figure uses mean side-hustle income; at the median it would take years, not months.

commonlyWrong.text: Unusual options-flow alerts reveal institutional orders that retail day traders can profitably follow
commonlyWrong.note: Order flow carries some information in academic data, but public flow alerts arrive late and noisy, and nothing shows retail traders profit from following them.

commonlyWrong.text: Wealth creation is positive-sum, so everyone can become wealthy
commonlyWrong.note: Total wealth grows, but being wealthy is largely relative and scarce assets are constrained, so positive-sum growth does not mean everyone can become wealthy.

commonlyWrong.text: Writing YouTube scripts with AI for other creators pays a reliable freelance income
commonlyWrong.note: Scriptwriting gigs exist, but freelance platforms are crowded, creators increasingly use AI themselves, and income for beginners is irregular rather than reliable.

commonlyWrong.text: YouTube ad revenue can become significant income once a channel is monetized.
commonlyWrong.note: Most monetized channels earn little from ads, so significant income is the exception rather than what monetization typically brings.

commonlyWrong.text: Credit card limits rise automatically even when the card is barely used
commonlyWrong.note: Issuers raise limits based on usage and payment history, and cut dormant lines.

commonlyWrong.text: Most of the very wealthy dropped out of college rather than graduating
commonlyWrong.note: Surveys of the ultra-wealthy show a large majority hold degrees, many from elite schools.

claim.text: There are no get-rich-quick schemes; whoever sells one is getting rich off the buyer
claim.note: FTC business-opportunity cases and MLM income disclosures consistently show the seller profits while most buyers lose money, though rare individual windfalls exist.

priorRecord.note: FTC business-opportunity cases and MLM income disclosures consistently show the seller profits while most buyers lose money, though rare individual windfalls exist.

evidenceRecord.note: Nudge took over $400 million in revenue from 2014-2017 selling house-flipping training while more than 95% of attendees paid more than they netted; one scheme illustrating the seller profiting at buyers' expense.

claim.text: Advice from people who got rich quickly is survivorship bias, like reading out winning lottery numbers
claim.note: Survivorship bias is well documented; the specific path of a rapid success rarely replicates because luck and timing dominated it.

priorRecord.note: Survivorship bias is well documented; the specific path of a rapid success rarely replicates because luck and timing dominated it.

evidenceRecord.note: Screening 53,038 listed firms' ROA over 1966-2008, the authors find that popular success books follow the recipe of picking the winners and abstracting their behaviour into principles without checking them against a reference population, and that only 9 of the 209 firms those nine books use as cases show ROA significantly better than their peers, so most lessons are drawn from performance indistinguishable from luck (firms and their management books, not people who got rich quickly, and it does not measure what happens to anyone who follows the advice).

claim.text: Making money is a learnable skill, not luck; a skilled person could rebuild wealth from nothing within a decade
claim.note: Skill raises the odds, but research on entrepreneurial and wealth outcomes finds a large luck component, so neither 'not luck' nor a reliable decade-long rebuild holds.

priorRecord.note: Skill raises the odds, but research on entrepreneurial and wealth outcomes finds a large luck component, so neither 'not luck' nor a reliable decade-long rebuild holds.

evidenceRecord.note: In the model skill raises the odds but is far from sufficient: medium-high talent is often necessary, yet the most talented agents (T > 0.8) are the top performer in only 3% of runs and only about a third of highly talented agents end above their starting capital, contradicting the skill-not-luck framing; rebuilding wealth in a decade is not modelled.

claim.text: Genuinely passive income is rare and only becomes possible after years of active, unglamorous income
claim.note: Passive income almost always requires accumulated capital or an operating business first; income disclosures from passive-income pitches show most buyers earn little.

priorRecord.note: Passive income almost always requires accumulated capital or an operating business first; income disclosures from passive-income pitches show most buyers earn little.

evidenceRecord.note: Automators sold 'completely passive' mailbox-money stores at $35,000-$65,000 and, per the FTC, most purchasers did not recoup their investment; supports that promised passive income rarely materialises, not the 'years of active income' mechanism.

claim.text: Entrepreneurship is often more of a prison than a 9-to-5 in its early years; the freedom narrative is oversold
claim.note: Self-employed people report longer hours, lower median income and higher financial stress than employees in most surveys.

priorRecord.note: Self-employed people report longer hours, lower median income and higher financial stress than employees in most surveys.

evidenceRecord.note: Incorporated self-employed work about 340 more hours a year than comparable full-time, full-year salaried workers (144 more within-person after fixed effects) and the unincorporated also work more than they did as employees, so self-employment brings a material jump in hours rather than freedom; the paper does not single out the early years.

claim.text: Prediction-market exchanges are structurally fairer than sportsbooks because the platform is not the counterparty and does not limit winners
claim.note: Sportsbooks demonstrably limit or close winning accounts, while exchanges match peers for a fee, though exchanges can still delist markets or change resolution rules.

priorRecord.note: Sportsbooks demonstrably limit or close winning accounts, while exchanges match peers for a fee, though exchanges can still delist markets or change resolution rules.

evidenceRecord.note: Retail options trades lost $1.14bn while $4.13bn of effective-spread costs became revenue for market makers and exchanges executing retail orders; the liquidity-provision mechanism is asserted rather than tested.

priorRecord.note: Salary aggregators sample employed or surviving traders only.

evidenceRecord.note: Day trading for a living is shown to be virtually impossible, contrary to what brokerage specialists and course providers often claim; the finding falsifies the promise without establishing intent to deceive.

claim.text: Income-scheme promoters target people under financial stress
claim.note: Complaint data show spikes in income-scam reports during downturns.

priorRecord.note: Complaint data show spikes in income-scam reports during downturns.

priorRecord.note: Sports outcomes have no formulaic probability; the vig hides the expected loss.

evidenceRecord.note: The conclusion recommends price transparency for complex bets that consumers find difficult to value accurately, supporting opacity for such bets, but the contrast with lotteries and slots is not examined.

claim.text: Retail options trading has grown many-fold since commission-free trading apps appeared

evidenceRecord.note: Dollar volume of retail-origin (SLAN) and small option trades grew 143% and 224% between Nov 2019 and Jul 2021; strong growth but the data start in 2019 so growth since 2015 is not measured.

claim.note: Kahneman and Klein's conditions for expertise and forecaster track-record studies support this.

priorRecord.note: Kahneman and Klein's conditions for expertise and forecaster track-record studies support this.

claim.text: Recruiting a downline gives MLM participants leverage and scalable income
claim.note: Downline-based commissions and rank bonuses exist, but the rank tables show over 90% of participants in the lowest cohort averaging under $100 while six-figure incomes belong to hundredths of a percent; the leverage is real only for a tiny fraction.

priorRecord.note: Income disclosures show downline earnings concentrate in the top one percent and the structure makes most downlines unprofitable.

evidenceRecord.note: Downline-based commissions and rank bonuses exist, but the rank tables show over 90% of participants in the lowest cohort averaging under $100 while six-figure incomes belong to hundredths of a percent; the leverage is real only for a tiny fraction.

claim.note: Even the best documented traders compound slowly; month-level outcomes for beginners are dominated by noise and losses.

priorRecord.note: Even the best documented traders compound slowly; month-level outcomes for beginners are dominated by noise and losses.

evidenceRecord.note: Only 15.5% of those who day traded 2-50 days ended with any positive net profit, and even the best long-run trader averaged US$310 a day; wealth after one month is not measured directly.

claim.text: Investors accept low expected returns on lottery-like assets because of the small chance of a huge payoff
claim.note: The skewness or lottery preference is a robust asset-pricing finding across stocks, options and other assets.

priorRecord.note: The skewness or lottery preference is a robust asset-pricing finding across stocks, options and other assets.

evidenceRecord.note: Crypto adoption responds less to price rises in more risk-averse countries and UK survey evidence cites 'a gamble that could make or lose money' as a main reason for buying, consistent with lottery-style motives, but expected returns are not measured.

claim.text: Copying the habits of successful people does not work because the unsuccessful share the same habits
claim.note: Selecting on the outcome makes habit correlations uninformative; base-rate failure data for founders and creators bears this out.

priorRecord.note: Selecting on the outcome makes habit correlations uninformative; base-rate failure data for founders and creators bears this out.

evidenceRecord.note: The popular success books never compare their chosen companies with a suitable reference population, so the behaviours they recommend were not shown to separate winners from others, and most of their 209 case firms perform indistinguishably from luck; this supports the reasoning for firms, but the paper does not measure whether unsuccessful firms or people share the same habits.

claim.text: The typical side hustle earns a few hundred dollars a month, far below the headline average
claim.note: Survey data consistently show heavily right-skewed side-hustle earnings with a low median.

priorRecord.note: Survey data consistently show heavily right-skewed side-hustle earnings with a low median.

evidenceRecord.note: For MLM specifically the typical participant earns far less than a few hundred a month: the vast majority received $1,000 or less per year (under $84/month) before expenses; MLM is one side-hustle type, so this narrows rather than tests the general claim.

contested.text: Advice from people who got rich quickly is survivorship bias, like reading out winning lottery numbers
contested.note: Survivorship bias is well documented; the specific path of a rapid success rarely replicates because luck and timing dominated it.

contested.text: Low-effort arbitrage pays only for early movers; once a method is widely taught, competition crowds out the returns
contested.note: Easily replicated strategies see returns compete away as entrants flood in, consistent with observed cycles in self-publishing and dropshipping niches.

contested.text: Most new YouTube channels earn nothing for months and most starters quit before growth arrives.
contested.note: The vast majority of channels never reach monetization thresholds; early view counts are typically near zero.

contested.text: Most MLM participants earn little or nothing and a substantial share lose money
contested.note: Of the 601 surveyed participants, 25% made any profit over their whole time in the MLM: 14% under $5,000, 6% $5,000 to $9,999, 3% $10,000 to $24,999, 3% $25,000 or more, and 3 people (0.5%) $100,000 or more; 47% lost money (41% under $5,000, 3% $5,000 to $9,999, 1% over $10,000) and 27% broke even; all self-reported.

contested.text: An established FBA business runs on a few hours a week of the owner's time
contested.note: Possible with paid staff and a mature product, but most sellers report more hands-on time and the setup labor is excluded.

contested.text: You cannot get rich by renting out your time; wealth requires owning equity in a business, product or asset
contested.note: Wealth surveys show most large fortunes come from business ownership and assets, but high-earning salaried professionals do accumulate wealth by saving and investing.

contested.text: Backtested candlestick patterns show no reliable edge.
contested.note: Academic tests of candlestick signals on major indices find no profitable predictive power after costs.

contested.text: Beginners following paid or community trade signals typically lose money
contested.note: First-hand tests and brokerage data lean to losses, but signal quality varies and samples are small.

contested.text: A few percent per day compounds to impossible annual returns, so such claimed trading rates cannot be sustained.
contested.note: Compounding arithmetic; no documented investor has sustained anything close.

contested.text: MLM income comes mainly from recruiting and leading a downline, not from selling product to retail customers
contested.note: All 30 MLMs with earnings data (and all 350 whose compensation plans Taylor reviewed) pay rewards primarily for recruiting a large downline, not for retailing products, with most payout going to the highest levels.

contested.text: Online side hustles fail without an owned audience because traffic is the real bottleneck
contested.note: Customer acquisition is the dominant cost in online business, but many profitable stores run on paid traffic without an audience; the audience framing suits a YouTube coach.

contested.text: Prop-firm evaluation challenges are structured so most participants pay fees and never get funded
contested.note: Firms' own and regulator disclosures show low pass rates and fee-driven revenue; some firms have been sanctioned.

contested.text: Short-term stock moves are unpredictable, so day trading is gambling
contested.note: Authors conclude that for prospective day traders trading to learn is no more rational or profitable than playing roulette, yet under 3% of traders are predictably profitable, so it is not pure chance.

contested.text: Demeaning salaried jobs and college is a sales tactic; both generally improve financial outcomes
contested.note: The college earnings premium and the stability of salaried work are well documented, though college is not right for everyone.

contested.text: Dropshipping can make an ordinary beginner a millionaire
contested.note: A few sellers reach that scale; the typical outcome is a loss, so the implied generality fails.

contested.text: Producing polished short-form content takes hours per video and is effectively a full-time job.
contested.note: Creator time-use reports consistently show planning, filming and editing dominate, far beyond the posted runtime.

contested.text: Profitable active trading is a full-time job needing research, data and infrastructure, not an evening hobby.
contested.note: Professional quant and discretionary shops run on teams and paid data; part-time retail traders underperform in brokerage studies.

contested.text: Rental property needs a large down payment plus cash reserves for repairs and vacancies
contested.note: Lenders require 15 to 25 percent down on investment property, and repairs and vacancies are routine costs.

contested.text: Retail traders bid up option prices before earnings announcements and lose when volatility subsides
contested.note: de Silva, Smith and So document retail losses of five to fourteen percent around earnings announcements from overpaying for implied volatility.

contested.text: Retail AI trading bots do not beat the market
contested.note: No retail trading bot has an audited record of beating the market; many are outright scams.

contested.text: A trader who is net profitable over ten tracked practice trades is ready to trade real money
contested.note: Ten trades is far too small a sample to distinguish an edge from luck; statistical tests of trading skill need hundreds of trades.

contested.text: Anyone can earn a large annual income by just earning a modest amount every day
contested.note: Dividing a target by days is arithmetic, not a method; median earnings show most people cannot sustain such a daily figure.

contested.text: Brands now get user-generated ad content from small accounts for free product or nothing.
contested.note: UGC marketplaces and gifting-only campaigns are standard practice; pay is low or in-kind for small creators.

contested.text: Buying the dip only works in an uptrending market; in a downtrend dip-buying loses money
contested.note: Trend-following has some empirical support, but defining the trend is only clear in hindsight, so the rule is hard to act on in real time.

contested.text: Celebrity endorsements are not evidence that a speculative asset is a sound investment
contested.note: Celebrity-promoted tokens have repeatedly collapsed and regulators have fined undisclosed paid promotions.

contested.text: Day traders do not improve with experience; the longer they trade, the less likely they are profitable
contested.note: Share of profitable day traders falls monotonically with days traded (29.8% to 3.0%) and fixed-effects panel regressions on persistent traders find no learning; expected profit stays negative.

contested.text: Hard money lenders require a down payment plus points, fees, and double-digit interest
contested.note: Typical hard money terms are 10-20% down, 2-4 points, and 10-14% interest.

contested.text: Most altcoins never reclaim their prior-cycle highs when measured in Bitcoin
contested.note: True of most large altcoins across the 2017 and 2021 cycles, with a few exceptions.

contested.text: Niche does not matter for short-form content because the creator's personality is the differentiator
contested.note: A framing about creative strategy with no clear evidence either way.

contested.text: Review swapping among course members to seed book reviews violates platform rules and risks account bans
contested.note: Major retailers prohibit reciprocal and incentivized reviews and have removed reviews and banned accounts for it.

contested.text: Sellers of money-making systems must have solid proof before making earnings claims
contested.note: The FTC Business Opportunity Rule bars earnings claims unless the seller has a reasonable basis, written substantiation, and gives prospects an earnings claim statement with the number and percentage of purchasers who achieved that level; a US legal requirement.

contested.text: Selling skill takes years of practice, not a five-day seminar
contested.note: Sales performance develops over years of practice; no short course has demonstrated otherwise.

thinEvidence.text: Targeting trades that pay twice what is risked lets a trader be wrong most of the time and still profit
thinEvidence.note: The arithmetic is correct, but win rate falls as reward targets widen, so a 2:1 target does not by itself make a trader profitable.

thinEvidence.text: Sustained moderate returns compounded for decades beat chasing the highest returns.
thinEvidence.note: Long-horizon wealth is dominated by time in market; high-return strategies tend to be unrepeatable or blow up.

thinEvidence.text: Luxury lifestyles displayed by gurus can be rented or faked
thinEvidence.note: Rented cars, houses and jets are documented in exposes of course sellers; the display proves nothing about income.

thinEvidence.text: Practicing in a simulator before trading real money improves a trader's odds
thinEvidence.note: Simulators teach mechanics and can screen out losing strategies, but they omit slippage and emotion and the large majority of day traders still lose money.

thinEvidence.text: The finance industry attracts hucksters promising outsized returns, so too-good-to-be-true pitches usually are.
thinEvidence.note: Regulatory enforcement records show investment fraud consistently among the largest consumer-loss categories.

thinEvidence.text: Most of what paid online courses teach is available free online
thinEvidence.note: Platform docs, free guides and videos cover the same material; the course adds structure, not secrets.

thinEvidence.text: Never bet everything on one gamble even with an edge, because ruin removes you from the game
thinEvidence.note: Kelly-criterion and ergodicity arguments show that full-stake bets with positive expectation still go bust with probability approaching one over repeated play.

thinEvidence.text: Paid-traffic dropshipping margins collapse as ad costs rise and competitors copy the product
thinEvidence.note: Low barriers to entry mean any winning product is cloned within weeks, and ad auctions price the margin away; this is the standard dropshipping failure mode.

thinEvidence.text: Selling AI automation setups to local small businesses is a viable low-capital service business because owners want AI but lack time to implement it
thinEvidence.note: It is a low-capital service and owners do show interest in AI, but demand, pricing and retention for one-person agencies are unproven.

thinEvidence.text: AI tools can build a dropshipping store, product pages and ads in hours instead of days
thinEvidence.note: Store builders, copy and image generators do produce a functional store quickly; whether it sells is a separate question.

thinEvidence.text: Funded-trader (prop firm) accounts let beginners trade size without their own capital
thinEvidence.note: Most evaluation-based prop firm customers fail and pay repeated fees, and few beginners ever trade funded size or get paid.

thinEvidence.text: Copying a proven competitor's product, page and ad angles is the fastest route to first sales
thinEvidence.note: Cloning validated offers does shortcut discovery, but it puts the copier in direct ad-auction competition with the original and fuels the race to the bottom.

thinEvidence.text: Digital products avoid suppliers and shipping and carry near-total margins
thinEvidence.note: Marginal cost is near zero; the cost shifts to creation and marketing.

thinEvidence.text: An established FBA business runs on a few hours a week of the owner's time
thinEvidence.note: Possible with paid staff and a mature product, but most sellers report more hands-on time and the setup labor is excluded.

thinEvidence.text: Faceless AI-generated YouTube channels get buried by the algorithm and demonetized, so they rarely make money
thinEvidence.note: The platform tightened monetization rules against mass-produced and repetitive content, though some AI-assisted channels still earn.

thinEvidence.text: A genuinely profitable short-term strategy is capacity-limited, so its owner would keep it secret rather than sell it.
thinEvidence.note: Quant funds routinely cap capacity and guard strategies; selling a capacity-limited edge destroys it, which makes advertised strategies suspect.

thinEvidence.text: Identifying crypto narratives early (AI agents, meme coins, new chains) is how investors capture outsized returns
thinEvidence.note: The winning examples are survivorship-selected; most narrative and meme tokens lose most of their value and retail buyers rarely get in early.

thinEvidence.text: Income from dividends or interest large enough to matter requires a capital base most beginners lack
thinEvidence.note: At typical 2-4% yields, a modest weekly income needs six figures invested, as the video's own arithmetic shows.

thinEvidence.text: Losses trigger revenge trading that compounds losses in an emotional feedback loop
thinEvidence.note: Behavioral-finance studies document loss-chasing and increased risk-taking after losses among retail traders.

thinEvidence.text: Most actively managed funds underperform index funds after fees
thinEvidence.note: SPIVA scorecards consistently show most active funds trailing their benchmarks over ten-plus years.

thinEvidence.text: Once a trader has a consistently profitable setup, profits scale by simply increasing position size
thinEvidence.note: Liquidity, slippage and market impact erode edges as size grows, especially in thin small caps, so profits do not scale by simply sizing up.

thinEvidence.text: Organic TikTok and Instagram content can sell dropshipped products with no ad spend
thinEvidence.note: Organic virality does produce sales for some stores, but reach is unpredictable and most organic posts sell little.

thinEvidence.text: Platform creator payouts are negligible for most creators even with large followings.
thinEvidence.note: Creator-economy surveys find median earnings from platform programs are tiny; meaningful income comes from brand deals or owned products.

thinEvidence.text: Product research tools showing live sales data let you validate demand before spending on ads
thinEvidence.note: These tools show that demand exists, but every subscriber sees the same products and existing sales do not predict a new store's conversion or ad cost.

thinEvidence.text: Self-made wealth accumulates slowly through compounding over a decade or more, not in one big payout
thinEvidence.note: Most self-made millionaires reach it in their 40s and 50s after decades of accumulation, though tech exits give a minority lumpy, lottery-like outcomes.

thinEvidence.text: Slow or unreliable supplier fulfillment kills dropshipping stores through refunds and chargebacks
thinEvidence.note: Long shipping times are the main driver of dropshipping disputes and payment-processor holds, which is well documented by platforms and sellers.

thinEvidence.text: TikTok Shop affiliate videos can earn beginners a full-time income from product commissions
thinEvidence.note: Affiliate commission income is heavily skewed: a few creators earn large sums while most affiliates earn little or nothing.

thinEvidence.text: Trading a funded prop-firm account can replace a full-time income
thinEvidence.note: Firms that disclosed data show only a small share of funded traders ever receive a payout, and fewer receive repeated ones.

thinEvidence.text: Trading psychology, especially accepting losses, is the main determinant of trading success
thinEvidence.note: Behavioural biases do hurt traders, but no amount of discipline creates an edge where none exists; psychology explains failure more than it produces success.

thinEvidence.text: Uploading self-published books to Amazon produces ongoing royalties with little further work
thinEvidence.note: The median self-published title earns almost nothing and the store is flooded with low-content books, so ongoing royalties with little work is not the typical result.

thinEvidence.text: YouTube income compounds because old videos keep generating views and sales years later
thinEvidence.note: Evergreen search-driven videos do keep earning, but most videos decay quickly, so compounding holds only for a minority of channels.

thinEvidence.text: Affiliate marketing and dropshipping are so saturated that newcomers rarely make money
thinEvidence.note: Both still produce income for some, but saturation and rising ad costs have cut newcomer odds; 'don't work' overstates it.

thinEvidence.text: Backtested candlestick patterns show no reliable edge.
thinEvidence.note: Academic tests of candlestick signals on major indices find no profitable predictive power after costs.

thinEvidence.text: Beginners following paid or community trade signals typically lose money
